Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt introduces space-tileable tensegrity metamaterials designed to delocalize deformation by introducing a discontinuity in their compression members. This architectural feature prevents continuous compressive paths, which in turn inhibits localized failure propagation and produces a homogeneous, delocalized deformation distribution. The authors report dramatic improvements over comparable-strength state-of-the-art lattice architectures: up to a 25-fold enhancement in deformability and "orders of magnitude" increases in energy absorption capability without failure. The paper contrasts these tensegrity metamaterials with conventional stretching-dominated lattice designs, which typically exhibit unstable post-yield behavior (negative stiffness events) and catastrophic collapse once loaded beyond initial peak strength. Thus, the tensegrity design is presented as a pathway to failure-resistant, high-energy-absorbing lightweight structures by avoiding localized deformation and system-level instability.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'rosa2024stiffanddeformable pages 12-14'.

Matheus I. N. Rosa, Konstantinos Karapiperis, Kaoutar Radi, and Dennis M. Kochmann. Stiff and deformable quasicrystalline architected materials. Preprint, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652. This article has 2 citations.

Rosa et al. report that quasi-periodic (quasicrystalline) dual-lattice architectures develop delocalized force-chain distributions that both increase stiffness and enable stable post-buckling deformation, avoiding the unstable collapse often observed in periodic stretching-dominated lattices. Experimentally these dual lattices show relatively high stiffness, superior elastic energy absorption, and enhanced failure resistance under cyclic loading. Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000049

From text 'schulerUnknownyearrecentbritishdevelopments pages 171-176'.

SC Schuler. Recent british developments in package cushioning, dynamic testing and instrumentation. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt describes laboratory rough-handling tests using loaded (payload-containing) containers subjected to free-fall and impact procedures. Drop modes include edgewise, cornerwise and flatwise drops: edgewise and cornerwise drops were performed from heights of 12, 24 and 36 inches to a metal surface; flatwise drops were from 6 and 12 inches to a metal surface. A pendulum impact uses a flat vertical metal barrier, with up to 2 inches of wood between barrier and container. The tests explicitly reference "loaded container" conditions, indicating payloads were present during impact. Instrumentation included three accelerometers (vertical, longitudinal, lateral) to capture vector shock components and calculation of resultant g by the square root of sum of squares. The excerpt therefore documents use of rigid metal impact surfaces (or metal barrier with limited wood padding) for drop and impact testing of loaded containers, rather than specifying concrete, and provides typical heights and measurement practice.


---

## pqac-00000050

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt discusses regulatory expectations for drop-test impact surfaces similar to ASTM D5276’s requirement that the impact surface be rigid/flat/unyielding. It cites UN/ADR/IMDG references and ISO 2248 specifications: the impact target should have mass at least 50 times the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤2 mm, and rigidity such that a 100 mm² area loaded with 10 kg produces ≤0.1 mm static deformation. The text stresses that test outcomes depend on how kinetic energy is partitioned between package and impact surface, and notes that current regulations lack guidance on transient dynamic response (stress wave propagation, eigenfrequencies). It also cites an alternative criterion used for radioactive material packaging: a reinforced concrete foundation with solidly anchored steel plate of combined mass ≥10× specimen, and research showing transmitted energy into the target/ground <2%. The common practical design is a reinforced concrete foundation with an anchored steel impact plate. The excerpt raises questions about whether a fixed mass ratio (50×) is decisive and whether alternative design parameters could be used.


---

## pqac-00000051

From text 'menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7'.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a guided drop-test setup that uses a very heavy, rigid impact foundation: "The foundation consists of a  steel-reinforced concrete block with an anchored steel impact pad and has a mass of 18 000 kg." The impact area is large and flat ("The impact area  is 2000  2000 mm.") and the apparatus design explicitly requires that "The impact must not be damped." and that fixtures avoid restraining deformation ("The important aspect of this ﬁxture is that the test objects are not supported in a way that would cause their deformation to be restrained."). Test specimens (jerrycans) were filled and secured during drops ("The jerrycan was ﬁxed with the use of slings to form a harness..."; "Careful attention was given to minimize the movement of the fluid, so the package was held in position." with fluid presence checked by "visually detected by watching the remaining air bubble space in the jerrycan"). These details align with key elements of ASTM D5276-style free-fall loaded-container testing: a rigid, unyielding impact surface and conducting drops with the payload present in the container.


---

## pqac-00000052

From text 'grabowskiUnknownyeardesignandevaluation pages 171-176'.

TJ Grabowski. Design and evaluation of packages containing cushioned items, using peak acceleration versus static stress data. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

Grabowski documents laboratory drop and impact tests on loaded containers where the package is allowed to fall freely onto rigid metal impact surfaces. Edgewise and cornerwise drops were performed from 12, 24 and 36 inches to a metal surface; flatwise drops from 6 and 12 inches to a metal surface. A pendulum impact used a flat, vertical, stationary metal barrier (with up to 2 in. of wood between barrier and container). Containers in these tests are explicitly described as "loaded" and were opened after testing to inspect container and contents. Shock measurement used three accelerometers (vertical, longitudinal, lateral) and computed a resultant impact by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the three components. The excerpt therefore describes using rigid metal impact surfaces and testing with payloads in the container, and quantifying shock via three-axis accelerometer data and vector resultant calculations.


---

## pqac-00000053

From text 'wood1965designcriteriatechnical pages 102-106'.

Charles W. Wood, John H. Watts, and Robert M. Lucas. Design criteria, technical characteristics, and design concepts for an air transportable container. ArXiv, Jun 1965. URL: https://doi.org/10.21236/ad0619158, doi:10.21236/ad0619158. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt discusses vibration and shock test criteria and the role of drop tests. It recommends a 12-g shock of 0.080–0.100 s as a design criterion and notes a suggested sinusoidal vibration test of 5 g in three directions from 1 to 1000 cps. The authors state that proof tests (usually drop tests) are the final confirmation of design. With reference to MIL-STD-810 Table 516-1, a 24-inch drop is cited as producing about 100 g. However, the authors caution that drop tests are primarily applicable to assessing the integrity of shock-protected equipment when accidentally dropped, and may not represent the specific structural design requirements for shipping containers aboard aircraft—drop tests confirm gross survivability rather than define container design. They also note practical testing limits: a fully loaded container at 5 g requires a very large vibration table, so often only critical parts or assemblies are tested in a jig. The excerpt does not explicitly state impact-surface materials (e.g., rigid concrete) nor an explicit requirement about leaving the payload inside the container for drop tests.

From text 'menrad2014droptestof pages 8-8'.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The study performed free‑fall drop tests on filled polyethylene jerrycans. Tests used jerrycans filled with glycol (cooled to ~20–23°C and kept below the cited test‑standard requirement of 18°C) and measured temperature immediately after impact. The test rig released the harnessed jerrycan while a wagon ran on rails; slings were arranged so they did not constrain deformation or damp impacts. Because the wagon carried significant kinetic energy, aluminium honeycomb plates were installed to absorb the wagon impact energy so the wagon would not strike the jerrycan. A tray beneath the sample to catch leaks had its bottom cut out and sealed specifically so the impact would not be damped and the jerrycan could strike the foundation directly. The authors note small variations in impact velocity from rail friction, tilt and splices, and chose the large side wall as the critical impact orientation. Drop heights reached an equivalent free‑fall height up to 7.1 m without causing failure.

However, it does not specify details about impact surface (e.g., rigid/unyielding concrete) or state requirements about payload being present in the container for drop testing; those specifics are not included in these pages.

Abstract:
More than four decades have passed since the introduction of safety standards for impact attenuation surfaces (IAS) used in playgrounds. Falls in children's playground are a major source of injuries and IAS is one of the best methods of preventing severe head injuries. However, the ability of IAS in prevention of other types of injuries, such as upper limb fractures, is unclear. Accordingly, in this paper, ten synthetic playground surfaces were tested to examine their performance beyond the collected head injury criterion (HIC) and maximum G-force (Gmax) outputs recommended by ASTM F1292. The aim of this work was to investigate any limitations with current safety criteria and proposing additional criteria to filter hazardous IAS that technically comply with the current 1000 HIC and 200 Gmax thresholds. The proposed new criterion is called the impulse force criterion (If). If combines two important injury predictor characteristics, namely: HIC duration that is time duration of the most severe impact; and the change in momentum that addresses the IAS properties associated with bounce. Additionally, the maximum jerk (Jmax), the bounce, and the IAS absorbed work are presented. HIC, Gmax, If, and Jmax followed similar trends regarding material thickness and drop height. Moreover, the bounce and work done by the IAS on the falling missile at increasing drop heights was similar for all surfaces apart from one viscoelastic foam sample. The results presented in this paper demonstrate the limitations of current safety criteria and should, therefore, assist future research to reduce long-bone injuries in playgrounds.

Abstract:
Research supports recess, however, playground injuries are prevalent with more than 200,000 cases per year requiring medical attention. School playgrounds are among the leading location for injury. The purpose was to identify the safety and risk factors of playground environments and impact attenuation characteristics of surfacing materials. Results demonstrated 46% playground spaces protected students from traffic. Results found 75% of playgrounds were exposed to full sun, and unitary surface materials were up to 49°F warmer than the air temperature. There was an increase in the probability of risk whether equipment height was over 9 ft for loose fill surfacing materials or over 6 ft for unitary surfaces. Loose strings or ropes looped over equipment were found on 23% of playgrounds. This study provides discussion and data pertaining to numerous aspects of playground safety. Strategies for school nurses are shared to shape policies and education for playground safety practices.

From text 'huber2001playgroundsurfacing pages 17-19'.

R Huber. Playground surfacing. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt summarizes key aspects of ASTM F1292 playground impact testing. The standard recognizes two equivalent test methods: ASTM F355 Procedure C (traditional) and the Free Fall Test Method. It measures two forces—Gmax and HIC—and considers three heights (Critical, Drop and Fall). Procedure C uses a head-shaped metal headform mounted to a rail or guide wires, instrumented with special electronic equipment; this instrumentation is described as cumbersome and expensive to deploy for field tests. A portable Free Fall Test instrument was developed and, per a six-laboratory round-robin, produced more repeatable/reproducible results than F355 Procedure C. Laboratory testing (including three-temperature tests) is used to determine the maximum drop height at which Gmax does not exceed 200 or HIC does not exceed 1000. Field tests at ambient temperature determine Gmax and HIC from the owner-specified drop height. The excerpt does not provide numeric headform mass or specific numeric drop heights for the Critical/Drop/Fall designations.

R Huber. Playground surfacing. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt summarizes key elements of ASTM F1292 Laboratory and free-fall (Annex A1) testing. Laboratory acceptance criteria require that, using an average of the last two of three drops, no value exceed 200 g-max or 1000 HIC for tests at 30, 72 and 120°F. Impact tests are performed in one-foot increments up to a maximum drop height, with three drops at each increment; tests are also performed one foot above and below the maximum. The drop height at which either Gmax or HIC is exceeded is taken as the system’s critical height. ## pqac-00000064

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 137-139'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt criticizes the ISO 2248 requirement that the impact target mass be at least 50 times the package (M/m ≥ 50), arguing this single mass-ratio rule does not assure a rigid, unyielding test surface and omits transient dynamic effects (kinetic energy transfer, energy restitution, ground strain). It recommends replacing the fixed mass-ratio requirement with technical criteria that consider the impact surface as an integrated foundation component whose geometry and mass must limit strain energy during the heaviest-package drop. Specific proposed provisions: (1) the impact surface must be part of a foundation behaving as a single mass with dimensions ensuring negligible strain energy; (2) if the impact surface component is <10% of total foundation thickness, only that component’s geometry is considered; (3) the required mass M should be determined via an energy-restitution-based factor α (so M ≥ α m) tied to a modified coefficient of restitution (e21), ground-strain limits, damping, and a safety factor. The approach allows estimating e21 from measured dmax or from initial shock response, making the mass-ratio requirement performance- and energy-based rather than a fixed number.

## pqac-00000065

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

Regulatory drop-test standards for dangerous goods (UN Model Regulations, ADR, RID, IMDG, IATA) require an essentially unyielding, horizontal, flat, immovable impact surface and reference ISO 2248 for detailed requirements. ISO 2248 (as cited) specifies: an impact target mass at least 50 times the heaviest package; flatness deviation not greater than 2 mm; rigidity such that static loading of 10 kg over 100 mm² causes no more than 0.1 mm deformation; and sufficient surface area for the package to land entirely on the plate. However, the regulations lack specifications for the dynamic mechanical response of the impact surface (transient impact loading, stress-wave propagation, eigenfrequencies), leaving potential ambiguity in design. For radioactive material (RAM) packaging, IAEA standards use a lower mass ratio (combined reinforced concrete foundation and steel plate at least 10 times the specimen) and studies have shown transmitted energy into the target/ground below ~2%, indicating practical unyielding behaviour. The excerpt notes practical problems for manufacturers who lack 50× foundations and highlights the need to consider alternative design parameters beyond a fixed mass ratio.


---

## pqac-00000066

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt summarizes ISO 2248 requirements and experimental validation for impact targets used in drop tests. ISO 2248 equivalence to a regulatory mass ratio is expressed as a maximum allowable energy transfer ratio δcrit = 1.96 %, which corresponds to an impact-target-to-package mass ratio M/m = 50 (worst-case complete energy transfer). The study used a steel plate (MIT–III) on the BAM foundation block as the impact plate and tested MITs with mass ratios of 15:1, 30:1 and 50:1; measured energy transfer percentages for these MITs were all well below the 1.96 % threshold, attributed to packaging deformation and dissipative filling. ISO 2248 also requires impact-surface flatness deviation not to exceed 2 mm; measured flatness values for MIT–I/II/III were 0.37, 0.25 and 0.22 mm respectively, meeting this criterion. Finally, ISO 2248 defines an "essentially unyielding" surface as deforming no more than xmax = 0.1 mm under a static 10 kg load applied over 100 mm2, a requirement used to assess local/global stiffness of impact surfaces.

## pqac-00000067

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 62-65'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt describes experimental model impact targets (MITs) used to study impact surface behavior in drop tests. MITs use three steel plates (280, 560, 980 kg) mounted on five low-damping spring elements and are tested against a fixed packaging gross mass of 18 kg, thereby exploring mass ratios up to roughly 54:1. Two complementary analysis approaches are used: (1) modal analysis and frequency response to establish rigidness criteria and thresholds for negligible elastic deformation so that energy restitution is dominated by the package, and (2) treating the impact pad plus subgrade as a rigid body oscillating vertically to evaluate maximum relative displacement and allowable kinetic energy. Numerical and experimental work aim to define a mass-ratio threshold between packaging and impact target, and to quantify kinetic energy dissipation through foundation and ground strain. Spring stiffness was chosen to limit dynamic displacement (noted target: 2 mm) to ensure minimal deflection. The excerpt does not explicitly cite ISO 2248 or state a prescriptive 50× mass ratio or a requirement for an unyielding concrete/steel plate, but it shows that the study intentionally includes a high (~50×) mass case and formulates criteria for what constitutes a sufficiently rigid impact surface.

The excerpt discusses how the required mass ratio for an impact surface to be considered essentially unyielding is determined by the restitution properties of the impact target and packaging together with the ground's dissipative properties (referenced to Equation 2.31). An energy-transfer threshold of 1.96% is used as a criterion. N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt describes Model Impact Targets (MITs) designed to be effectively rigid for package drop tests. Three steel-plate MITs (1 m × 1 m plates with thicknesses up to 0.120 m) have masses of 280, 560 and 960 kg. The test package gross mass is 18 kg, so the heaviest MIT produces a mass ratio of roughly 960/18 ≈ 53:1 (i.e., greater than 50:1). For each metric, indicate whether it is primarily dominated by payload mass/mounting or by the tensegrity cell itself, how faithful a no-payload simulation would be, whether post-hoc rescaling is feasible, and cite the relevant sources from the evidence gathered (Zhang 2022, Agogino 2018, Pajunen 2019, Bauer 2021, Bayandor 2017, Vespignani 2018, Zhong 2013, Gao 2018, Goyal 1997, Joodaky 2020)."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Metric | Dominated By (Payload vs Cell) | No-Payload Simulation Fidelity | Rescaling Feasibility | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peak deceleration ($g_{max}$) | Usually payload mass + mounting stiffness once the payload is in the load path; cell topology/orientation still matters because it sets stopping distance and effective stiffness. Suspended payloads are especially payload-dominated; distributed/axial loading is more mixed. | **Moderate** for axial-load or distributed-inertia cases; **poor** for internally suspended payloads, where omission can underpredict internal relative motion or miss secondary impacts. | **Good** if response is close to SDOF and mounting stiffness is known: $g_{max}\sim \omega_n V$ or can be re-fit with effective $m$-$k$-$c$ from contact time and restitution; weak if strong mode switching or slack/tendon collision occurs. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031) |
| Pulse FWHM | Mixed, but more cell-dominated than $g_{max}$ because it tracks global compliance/stroke; payload mass lengthens the pulse when it increases effective inertia, while stiff mounting shortens it. | **Moderate to good** for rigidly attached or axially applied payloads if geometry/orientation are preserved; **poor to moderate** for soft suspended payloads because internal oscillation can split or broaden the pulse. | **Moderate** via equivalent $m$-$k$-$c$ calibration from measured contact time $t_c$ and restitution; weaker when multiple pulses arise from rebound or internal collisions. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028) |
| Specific energy absorption (SEA) | Primarily cell/material/topology-dominated when defined per protector mass; payload changes the operating point and total absorbed energy but not the intrinsic absorber mass basis. | **Good** for ranking architectures/topologies and protector concepts; **moderate** for predicting absolute absorbed energy in a payload-qualified test. | **Moderate** by scaling input energy $mgh$ or $\tfrac12 mV^2$ at fixed protector mass; not sufficient if payload changes deformation pathway or densification onset. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000039) |
| Volumetric efficiency ($\eta_V$) | Mostly cell-dominated because it is governed by geometry, available stroke, and deformation delocalization; payload mainly selects where on the response curve the cell operates. | **High** for topology screening and geometric comparisons, provided bounding volume and impact orientation are matched. | **Limited to moderate**; can scale with absorbed energy at common volume, but payload-induced localization or bottoming can shift the ranking near densification. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) |
| Force-time history shape | Strongly mixed: early contact and plateau behavior are cell-dominated, but payload mass/mounting strongly affect peak count, secondary lobes, rebound, and shock-pulse shape. Suspended payloads can create multimodal or double-hit signatures. | **Moderate** for bare-cell contact mechanics and load-limiting plateaus; **poor** for predicting full waveform under suspended or off-CG payloads. | **Moderate** with SRS/SDOF or equivalent-drop methods for single-mode pulses; **poor** for multi-lobed histories with slack tendons, internal impacts, or secondary contact. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) |
| Contact-patch evolution | Primarily cell-dominated through orientation, rod/endcap geometry, and global compliance; payload affects patch indirectly by changing attitude evolution and local load concentration. | **Good** for bare-cell orientation studies and topology screening if mass distribution is not drastically altered; **moderate to poor** when payload shifts CG enough to change landing attitude or induce floor pull-through artifacts. | **Poor to limited**; post-hoc scaling cannot reliably recover altered contact sequence once the payload changes attitude dynamics or local indentation sequence. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021) |
| Tendon strain energy distribution | Strongly cell- and topology-dominated for the main cage, but very payload-dominated for any dedicated suspension tendons. Soft suspended payloads can siphon energy into a drum mode and create large asymmetries. | **Good** for main-cage tendon ranking in bare-cell screens; **poor** for internal-suspension designs because the omitted payload removes the very tendons and energy path of interest. | **Limited** for main cage via effective stiffness updates; **poor** for suspended payload architectures because energy partition among cage vs suspension tendons is topology-specific and nonlinear. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| Modal response (drum mode of suspended payload vs cell breathing mode) | Dominated by the relative stiffness/mass ratio between payload suspension and cell. Cell breathing modes are cell-dominated; suspended-payload drum modes are payload-dominated and can overwhelm global impact response when frequencies are comparable. | **High** for breathing-mode identification of the bare cell; **very poor** as a surrogate for suspended-payload dynamics because omitting the payload deletes the critical internal mode. | **Moderate** only if modal separation is clear and a two-DOF model is adequate; **poor** when frequencies are close, tendons go slack, or internal collisions occur. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |


*Table: This table summarizes which drop-response metrics are governed mainly by the payload versus the tensegrity cell, how trustworthy bare-cell simulations are for each metric, and when post-hoc rescaling is plausible. It is useful for deciding what can be screened without payload and what must be simulated or tested with the payload in the load path.*

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1

        - TREATMENT: Treatment

Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).

created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We are running tensegrity drop simulations (MuJoCo, Newton/Warp, PolyFEM+IPC)
and planning matching physical drop tests on a class-1 T-prism: 3 PLA struts
(rho ~ 1240 kg/m^3, E ~ 3.5 GPa) and 9 TPU 85A tendons (NinjaFlex-class:
E ~ 12 MPa secant, sigma_break ~ 26 MPa, rho ~ 1200 kg/m^3). Two regimes are
clamped to a Lansmont M23 envelope:

- `crutch_tip` (issue #18): 75 kg static payload through a Ø24 mm x 25 mm cell,
  impact velocity 1.4 m/s (~0.1 m drop), peak target <= 8 g (HAVS),
  pulse >= 5 ms.
- `nasa_lander` (issues #14, #16): 5 kg payload through a Ø200 mm x 200 mm cell,
  impact velocity 9.8 m/s (M23 max delta-V), peak target <= 1500 g (GSFC GEVS).

We have struggled with visualisation/simulation realism when the payload is
included. With the SUPERball / NASA-TBR architecture (payload sphere suspended
inside the cage by 6 additional TPU tendons), the soft 12 MPa TPU 85A
suspension oscillated wildly at impact and yanked the 0.7 g prism through the
rigid floor in MuJoCo. With the payload distributed across the struts as added
inertia (axial-load model, matching a crutch tip), the renders are stable and
look physical. The bare prism (no payload, just intrinsic strut/tendon mass)
is also stable. A reviewer therefore asked: **for these drop-tests, can we
just leave the payload off in the simulations**, and what does that cost us in
real-world applicability?

Please produce an in-depth, citation-rich brief that answers:

# 1. Physics of payload inclusion in drop simulations

  (a) Which impact-response metrics are dominated by the payload (mass,
      mounting, suspension stiffness) and which are dominated by the
      tensegrity cell itself? Cover at minimum: peak deceleration (g_max),
      pulse FWHM, specific energy absorption (SEA = E_abs / m_protector),
      volumetric efficiency (eta_V), force-time history shape, contact-
      patch evolution, tendon strain energy distribution, and modal
      response (drum-mode of suspended payload vs cell breathing mode).

  (b) For each of these four mounting modes, give the expected physical
      regimes in which the simulation/experiment **with no payload** is
      a faithful surrogate, and the regimes in which it is misleading
      (state explicit thresholds where possible):

      A. Axially-loaded strut tip (crutch use case, payload via tip).
      B. Payload rigidly clamped to one strut (instrumented accelerometer
         mass on a strut, common in tensegrity-robotics drop logs).
      C. Payload suspended inside the cage by additional TPU tendons
         (SUPERball v1/v2 + NASA-TBR planetary lander style).
      D. Bare cell + fictitious added inertia ("topology screen").

  (c) Quantify the regime where a no-payload simulation can be rescaled
      post-hoc to predict the payload-laden response (e.g. via lumped
      Maxwell/Kelvin models, m_eff = m_payload + alpha*m_strut, or
      shock-response-spectrum convolution). Cite analytic and empirical
      precedents.

  (d) For TPU 85A tendons specifically (E ~ 12 MPa, very soft), what
      stiffness/mass ratio thresholds set the boundary between "cell-
      dominated" and "payload-dominated" response? Provide closed-form or
      tabulated guidance keyed to k_cable, m_payload, drop height.

# 2. Real-world applicability and standards mapping

  (a) Which ASTM and equivalent standards explicitly require the payload
      to be in the load path during the drop, and which permit (or
      require) bare-package drops? Cover at minimum: ASTM D5276 (free-fall
      drop of loaded containers, **rigid concrete or steel impact surface**,
      preconditioning, drop orientations), ASTM F1292 (playground impact
      attenuation, instrumented headform), ASTM F2971 (AM test reporting),
      ISTA 1A/1H, MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8 (transit/crash hazard),
      GSFC GEVS-STD-7000B (spacecraft), and any applicable JEDEC (#28
      Lansmont M23 family), ANSI/AAMI, ISO 4180. For each, list:
      load condition, impact surface specification (concrete vs steel vs
      compliant plate), required payload representation (real vs surrogate
      mass vs mass-and-CG), instrumentation, and acceptance criteria.

  (b) What is the convention in published tensegrity drop literature on
      reporting payload-vs-no-payload? Cover Zhang 2018 (icosahedron,
      114.9 g -> 40.9-46.5 g, 1 m), Zhang 2022 (22-inch, 235 g peak, 20 m,
      20-drop life), Agogino 2018 NASA SUPERball, Vespignani 2018 SUPERball
      v2, Anand 2022 (75 m biodegradable), Pajunen 2019 (24-impact reuse),
      Bauer 2021 (octet vs tensegrity localisation), MER airbag papers,
      and BEAR / Snapp 2024 / Gongora 2020-2022. Indicate where the
      drop was with or without a representative payload, and what
      mass-and-CG surrogate (if any) was used.

  (c) For our two regimes specifically: does ASTM D5276 (for crutch /
      packaging) or GEVS (for the NASA-lander regime) require a
      representative payload? On what impact surface (we currently model
      a rigid MuJoCo floor; the standards typically call out a *rigid
      concrete pad >= 150 mm thick on a >= 1 m^3 concrete or steel
      base*)?

  (d) Egg-drop demo path (#46/#47): can the payload-free simulation be
      defended publicly as predictive of the egg-laden drop, or must we
      bring the egg/cradle into both the simulation and the experiment?
      The PR #47 follow-up (`f41b7034`) protocol shared a Ø 200 mm bounding
      sphere, m_sys <= 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per
      ASTM D5276; how should that protocol be amended if we want to use
      bare-cell simulations as the screening tier?

# 3. Recommendations and decision rules

  (a) State an explicit rule-of-thumb for when each of the four mounting
      modes (A-D above) is appropriate at simulation-tier C
      (MuJoCo/NTRT rigid screening), tier B (DiffPD/Newton mid-fidelity),
      and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC high-fidelity).

  (b) Give 5-10 concrete simulation/experimental design changes to our
      current setup that would maximise the predictive value of *bare-cell*
      drop simulations while leaving the eventual *payload-laden* drop
      experiment defensible (e.g. always co-report m_eff = m_cell +
      m_payload, always run a 2-point payload-sensitivity sweep, always
      simulate on a rigid concrete-equivalent floor with stated E and rho,
      tie GEVS / D5276 floor surface specs to MuJoCo solref/solimp, etc.).

  (c) For the rigid floor model: what concrete-pad parameters should we
      use in MuJoCo / PolyFEM+IPC to be representative of the ASTM D5276
      and GEVS floor? Give: target Young's modulus, density, restitution,
      friction, surface roughness, contact stiffness in MuJoCo's
      solref/solimp normalisation (current is solref="0.002 1",
      solimp="0.98 0.999 0.0001"), and PolyFEM dhat / IPC barrier
      parameters.

  (d) Provide a one-paragraph defensible answer we can paste into the PR
      saying "yes, leave the payload off for now in the sim because X,
      but plan to bring it in at tier B/A and at the physical drop because
      Y, and here is the floor surface spec we are using to match D5276 /
      GEVS".

Please cite peer-reviewed sources for every numerical claim and explicitly
flag where the answer is engineering judgement vs literature-grounded.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

The prototype features a fully actuated six-bar design (24 actuators), compliant nylon cables (up to 15% stretch), torque-control enabled motors, and a robust mechanical structure capable of surviving impact velocities upwards of 8 m/s.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Flying robots are becoming increasingly widespread, not only as remote‐vision agents but also as tools capable of physically interacting with our world. As robots fly closer to obstacles, the likelihood of collision rises. While collision resilience solutions have been proposed for multirotor technology successfully, drones which rely on wings for much higher efficiency cannot sustain impacts without damage. Based on biological cues from woodpeckers, this article proposes a design approach to impact management which revolves around two new components. Head‐on collisions are handled by the robot's fuselage, replicating the brain‐protecting function of a woodpecker as it pecks a tree. Meanwhile, wing‐strike damage is mitigated with shoulder‐like structures. It is shown how these components can be implemented using tensegrity structures—the most optimal strength‐to‐weight architecture element—permitting tunable stiffness of joints and collision resilience. Optimization and manufacturing of these challenging structures as fuselage and wing joints are discussed. The approach is validated through integration into a fully flight‐capable robot, which is impact‐tested in controlled conditions and in outdoor environments. This method shows how tensegrity structures can be employed in flying robotics and paves the way toward winged drones safely operating in cluttered, contact‐prone environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Animals can finely modulate their leg stiffness to interact with complex terrains and absorb sudden shocks. In feats like leaping and sprinting, animals demonstrate a sophisticated interplay of opposing muscle pairs that actively modulate joint stiffness, while tendons and ligaments act as biological springs storing and releasing energy. Although legged robots have achieved notable progress in robust locomotion, they still lack the refined adaptability inherent in animal motor control. Integrating mechanisms that allow active control of leg stiffness presents a pathway towards more resilient robotic systems.This paper proposes a novel mechanical design to integrate compliancy into robot legs based on tensegrity - a structural principle that combines flexible cables and rigid elements to balance tension and compression. Tensegrity structures naturally allow for passive compliance, making them well-suited for absorbing impacts and adapting to diverse terrains. Our design features a robot leg with tensegrity joints and a mechanism to control the joint’s rotational stiffness by modulating the tension of the cable actuation system. We demonstrate that the robot leg can reduce the impact forces of sudden shocks by at least 34.7 % and achieve a similar leg flexion under a load difference of 10.26 N by adjusting its stiffness configuration. The results indicate that tensegrity-based leg designs harbors potential towards more resilient and adaptable legged robots.

Abstract:
Tensegrity robots, which are prototypical examples of hybrid soft–rigid robots, exhibit dynamical properties that provide ruggedness and adaptability. They also bring about, however, major challenges for locomotion control. Owing to high dimensionality and the complex evolution of contact states, data-driven approaches are appropriate for producing viable feedback policies for tensegrities. Guided policy search (GPS), a sample-efficient hybrid framework for optimization and reinforcement learning, has previously been applied to generate periodic, axis-constrained locomotion by an icosahedral tensegrity on flat ground. Varying environments and tasks, however, create a need for more adaptive and general locomotion control that actively utilizes an expanded space of robot states. This implies significantly higher needs in terms of sample data and setup effort. This work mitigates such requirements by proposing a new GPS -based reinforcement learning pipeline, which exploits the vehicle’s high degree of symmetry and appropriately learns contextual behaviors that are sustainable without periodicity. Newly achieved capabilities include axially unconstrained rolling, rough terrain traversal, and rough incline ascent. These tasks are evaluated for a small variety of key model parameters in simulation and tested on the NASA hardware prototype, SUPERball. Results confirm the utility of symmetry exploitation and the adaptability of the vehicle. They also shed light on numerous strengths and limitations of the GPS framework for policy design and transfer to real hybrid soft–rigid robots.

Abstract:
With the continued interest in scientific space exploration and rapid development of the commercialized space sector, there have been a wide array of exploration technologies proposed for planetary mobility. This paper aims to survey these new technologies, explain the motivations and challenges of traversing different space environments, and describe why certain approaches will be more ubiquitous. A continued dominance by four- and six-wheeled vehicles for lunar and Martian exploration due to reliability, simplicity, and efficiency is observed. However, there is an emergence of alternative wheeled vehicle kinematics, other legged locomotion, and flying, climbing, or hopping robots when these designs confer specific advantages. The engineering maxim “form follows function” is strongly represented within the array of robotic planetary explorer designs. The limitations of an irradiated, dusty, vacuous, remote operating environment which prioritizes efficiency and robust operation often lead to small iterations on working designs because deviations from the status quo are simply not feasible or deemed too risky. Those proposed designs which do deviate have clear justifications driven by their particular environments or intended purpose. Engineers developing future planetary exploring robots for space environments may find these considerations useful.

Abstract:
With the purpose of making soft robotic structures with embedded sensors, additive manufacturing techniques like fused deposition modeling (FDM) are popular. Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) filaments, with and without conductive fillers, are now commercially available. However, conventional FDM still has some limitations because of the marginal compatibility with soft materials. Material selection criteria for the available material options for FDM have not been established. In this study, an open-source soft robotic gripper design has been used to evaluate the FDM printing of TPU structures with integrated strain sensing elements in order to provide some guidelines for the material selection when an elastomer and a soft piezoresistive sensor are combined. Such soft grippers, with integrated strain sensing elements, were successfully printed using a multi-material FDM 3D printer. Characterization of the integrated piezoresistive sensor function, using dynamic tensile testing, revealed that the sensors exhibited good linearity up to 30% strain, which was sufficient for the deformation range of the selected gripper structure. Grippers produced using four different TPU materials were used to investigate the effect of the Shore hardness of the TPU on the piezoresistive sensor properties. The results indicated that the in situ printed strain sensing elements on the soft gripper were able to detect the deformation of the structure when the tentacles of the gripper were open or closed. The sensor signal could differentiate between the picking of small or big objects and when an obstacle prevented the tentacles from opening. Interestingly, the sensors embedded in the tentacles exhibited good reproducibility and linearity, and the sensitivity of the sensor response changed with the Shore hardness of the gripper. Correlation between TPU Shore hardness, used for the gripper body and sensitivity of the integrated in situ strain sensing elements, showed that material selection affects the sensor signal significantly.

Abstract:
Herein, the development of complex 3D intelligent structures such as robotic hands using innovative designs and multimaterial additive manufacturing technology is presented. The distal phalanges of the 3D printed hand presented herein have inherent soft capacitive touch or pressure sensors and embedded electronics. Materials such as thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), silver paint, conductive polylactic acid composite, graphite ink, etc. are explored to develop five different variants of the sensors using a modified 3D printer, which is capable of extruding conductive ink, metal paste, and polymers. The best‐performing 3D printed soft capacitive touch sensors, formed with silver paint and soft rubber (Ecoflex 00‐30), are integrated on the distal phalanges of the 3D printed robotic hand. These sensors exhibit a stable response with sensitivity of 0.00348 kPa−1 for pressure <10 kPa and 0.00134 kPa−1 for higher pressure. To demonstrate the practical applicability, the 3D printed hand with embedded soft capacitive touch sensors is used for interacting with everyday objects. The tightly integrated sensing elements within the 3D printed structures, as presented herein, can pave the way for a new generation of truly smart material systems that can possibly change their appearance and shape autonomously.

Abstract:
<jats:p xml:lang="en">Dynamic behavior of a wall-mounted air conditioner indoor unit is analyzed under drop impact condition. For simulation analysis, a finite element analysis code, known as Ansys Autodyn, is used. Physical drop tests are performed according to ASTM D5276 and ASTM D880 standards and strain gauges are used to measure the effective strains by attaching to specific areas subjected to excessive deformation. By recording drop test with high speed camera, the impact contact duration is also detected. By comparing experimental and numerical results, the validation of finite element analysis is performed. Product improvements are made for the damaged areas and validated by drop test. Conducting physical drop tests with strain gauges together with finite element analysis decreases product development lead time, reduces development costs and eliminates the product’s potential risks in advance. The approach presented with this work can be a reference guide for assessing the dynamic response of impact sensitive home and industrials applicants.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Engineering systems are often subject to complex loading mechanisms including accelerated mechanical shock during transportation, handling, and operations. Shock can be understood as a drastic, irregular change in acceleration experienced by an object due to impact at a very short period. This paper presents a preliminary study of the crashworthiness properties of in-service industrial marine fenders (or bumpers) intended for shock energy absorption. The peak accelerations (Gpeak) of the test specimens are experimentally measured and compared to theoretical estimations. The energy absorptions and impact forces of the test specimens are calculated using analytical formulations. The effects of introducing tubular through-holes in the specimens on the resulting peak accelerations and thereby the shock energy absorbing capacities are also investigated. Test specimens of thicknesses ranging between 10 mm and 30 mm are subjected to half-sine shock waves between 50G and 70G, which are generated by dropping a 5-kg payload from different heights ranging from 150 mm to 280 mm onto a padded shock seat for a pulse duration between 5 and 8 ms. The analytically determined Gpeak agrees well with the experimental values. It is found that the through-holes specimens with lower Gpeak, resisted smaller impact forces and absorbed up to 12% lesser energy per unit mass than their solid counterparts.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The demand for UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) has drastically increased within the past few years, with proven efficiency for remote sensing use. This paper analyses the feasibility of utilizing recycled plastics from bottles such as, Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) as 3D printing filament, in order to rapidly print foldable UAV airframes for remote sensing use. Previous work has failed to effectively address the process of 3D printing UAVs with a lack of literature pertaining to the ability of 3D printing UAVs with recycled materials and the environmental effects associated with this. To address this issue, this paper presents results analyzing the material properties of commonly used 3D printing filaments with that of the recycled filament, which has proven to be effective in use for this application. This new approach in manufacturing UAVs is expected to significantly benefit the low-cost manufacturing of UAVs, reducing the time taken to obtain UAVs, expanding the operational scope of these systems all whilst reducing the detrimental effects to the environment without any loss of functionality.

    author = "Paulus, Anselm and Geist, A. R. and Schumacher, Pierre and Musil, Vít and Martius, Georg",
    title = "Hard Contacts with Soft Gradients: Refining Differentiable Simulators for Learning and Control",
    year = "2025",
    journal = "ArXiv",
    volume = "abs/2506.14186",

    doi = "10.48550/arxiv.2506.14186",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2506.14186"
}


Abstract:
Contact forces pose a major challenge for gradient-based optimization of robot dynamics as they introduce jumps in the system's velocities. Penalty-based simulators, such as MuJoCo, simplify gradient computation by softening the contact forces. However, realistically simulating hard contacts requires very stiff contact settings, which leads to incorrect gradients when using automatic differentiation. On the other hand, using non-stiff settings strongly increases the sim-to-real gap. We analyze the contact computation of penalty-based simulators to identify the causes of gradient errors. Then, we propose DiffMJX, which combines adaptive integration with MuJoCo XLA, to notably improve gradient quality in the presence of hard contacts. Finally, we address a key limitation of contact gradients: they vanish when objects do not touch. To overcome this, we introduce Contacts From Distance (CFD), a mechanism that enables the simulator to generate informative contact gradients even before objects are in contact. To preserve physical realism, we apply CFD only in the backward pass using a straight-through trick, allowing us to compute useful gradients without modifying the forward simulation.

Tensegrity Metamaterials: Toward Failure‐Resistant Engineering Systems through Delocalized Deformation Valid Text Names: 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 3-6', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 7-8', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 8-9', 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 9-9' BibTex: @article{bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward, author = "Bauer, Jens and Kraus, Julie A. and Crook, Cameron and Rimoli, Julian J. and Valdevit, Lorenzo", title = "Tensegrity Metamaterials: Toward Failure‐Resistant Engineering Systems through Delocalized Deformation", year = "2021", journal = "Advanced Materials", volume = "33", month = "Feb", doi = "10.1002/adma.202005647", url = "https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647", publisher = "Wiley", issue = "10", issn = "0935-9648" } Abstract: Failure of materials and structures is inherently linked to localized mechanisms, from shear banding in metals, to crack propagation in ceramics and collapse of space‐trusses after buckling of individual struts. In lightweight structures, localized deformation causes catastrophic failure, limiting their application to small strain regimes. To ensure robustness under real‐world nonlinear loading scenarios, overdesigned linear‐elastic constructions are adopted. Here, the concept of delocalized deformation as a pathway to failure‐resistant structures and materials is introduced. Space‐tileable tensegrity metamaterials achieving delocalized deformation via the discontinuity of their compression members are presented. Unprecedented failure resistance is shown, with up to 25‐fold enhancement in deformability and orders of magnitude increased energy absorption capability without failure over same‐strength state‐of‐the‐art lattice architectures. This study provides important groundwork for design of superior engineering systems, from reusable impact protection systems to adaptive load‐bearing structures. Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials Valid Text Names: 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 1-2', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 2-4', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 4-5', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 5-8', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 8-9', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 9-10', 'ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity pages 10-10' BibTex: @article{ruffini2026asymmetrictension–compressionconnectivity, author = "Ruffini, Franco N. and Rimoli, Julian J.", title = "Asymmetric tension–compression connectivity governs deformation delocalization in truss-based metamaterials", year = "2026", journal = "npj Metamaterials", volume = "2", month = "Mar", doi = "10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1", url = "https://doi.org/10.1038/s44455-026-00020-1" } Abstract: Abstract

Failure in most material systems is characterized by strain localization, where deformation concentrates within a narrow region. Recently, a class of truss-based metamaterials has been shown to undergo severe deformation without exhibiting localization [1]. The mechanisms underlying this unusual delocalized response remain unknown. Here, we employ graph theory to elucidate the origins of this behavior. Each lattice is represented as a pair of graphs—the tension and compression networks—and their topological properties are quantified using graph-theoretic metrics. We find that the onset of localization correlates strongly with connectivity measures of these graphs. Specifically, deformation delocalization arises from an asymmetry in connectivity between these networks: when the tension graph remains more connected than the compression graph, deformation spreads throughout the structure instead of localizing. Connectivity measures such as average global efficiency[2] capture this transition quantitatively. This framework provides design principles for creating materials and metamaterials that intrinsically resist failure localization.

Relevant Snippet: … In lattice-based metamaterials, localization typically … equilibrium conditions in an ideal tensegrity structure, whereas in … truss-based metamaterials—the Kelvin and Octet lattices—were … --- ## 5. Bio-Inspired Curved-Elliptical Lattice Structures for Enhanced Mechanical Performance and Deformation Stability Valid Text Names: 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 1-2', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 2-4', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 4-6', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 6-9', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 9-11', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 11-13', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 13-15', 'guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice pages 15-15' BibTex: @article{guo2024bioinspiredcurvedellipticallattice, author = "Guo, Zhengmiao and Yang, Fan and Li, Lingbo and Wu, Jiacheng", title = "Bio-Inspired Curved-Elliptical Lattice Structures for Enhanced Mechanical Performance and Deformation Stability", year = "2024", journal = "Materials", volume = "17", pages = "4191", month = "Aug", doi = "10.3390/ma17174191", url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17174191", publisher = "MDPI AG", issue = "17", issn = "1996-1944" } Abstract: Lattice structures, characterized by their lightweight nature, high specific mechanical properties, and high design flexibility, have found widespread applications in fields such as aerospace and automotive engineering. However, the lightweight design of lattice structures often presents a trade-off between strength and stiffness. To tackle this issue, a bio-inspired curved-elliptical (BCE) lattice is proposed to enhance the mechanical performance and deformation stability of three-dimensional lattice structures. BCE lattice specimens with different parameters were fabricated using selective laser melting (SLM) technology, followed by quasi-static compression tests. Finite element (FE) numerical simulations were also carried out for validation. The results demonstrate that the proposed BCE lattice structures exhibit stronger mechanical performance and more stable deformation modes that can be adjusted through parameter tuning. Specifically, by adjusting the design parameters, the BCE lattice structure can exhibit a bending-dominated delocalized deformation mode, avoiding catastrophic collapse during deformation. The specific energy absorption (SEA) can reach 24.6 J/g at a relative density of only 8%, with enhancements of 48.5% and 297.6% compared with the traditional energy-absorbing lattices Octet and body-center cubic (BCC), respectively. Moreover, the crushing force efficiency (CFE) of the BCE lattice structure surpasses those of Octet and BCC by 34.9% and 15.8%, respectively. Through a parametric study of the influence of the number of peaks N and the curve amplitude A on the compression performance of the BCE lattice structure, the compression deformation mechanism is further analyzed. The results indicate that the curve amplitude A and the number of peaks N have significant impacts on the deformation mode of the BCE lattice. By adjusting the parameters N and A, a structure with a combination of high energy absorption, high stiffness, and strong fracture resistance can be obtained, integrating the advantages of tensile-dominated and bending-dominated lattice structures. We demonstrate that shape-memory protein–polymer networks can unravel to release their stored length and, after recovery, will reconfigure to accommodate higher loads. These materials are incorporated into lattice frameworks using additive manufacturing which are then shown to become up to 2.5× stiffer after being crushed to 80% strain and recovered. This strain learning behavior enables the creation of metamaterials that are “teachable” and can autonomously remodel in response to applied loads, similar to the processes that occur in natural materials. ## pqac-00000014

From text 'grabowskiUnknownyeardesignandevaluation pages 171-176'.

TJ Grabowski. Design and evaluation of packages containing cushioned items, using peak acceleration versus static stress data. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt describes laboratory handling tests on loaded containers including edgewise, cornerwise, flatwise drops and pendulum impact. Edgewise and cornerwise drops used the loaded container supported and allowed to drop to a metal surface from heights of 12, 24 and 36 inches. Flatwise drops were performed once each from 6 and 12 inches to a metal surface. Pendulum impact used a suspended container pulled back to a height (noted as 18 inches plus floor clearance) to strike a flat vertical metal barrier; a 2-inch maximum thickness of wood was placed between the barrier and container. The study records shock with three accelerometers mounted to capture vertical, longitudinal and lateral axes, and computes resultant impact as the square root of the sum of squares of the three components. After testing, containers were opened for visual inspection to check for interference or damage to container or contents. The excerpt does not specify concrete pad thickness, explicit payload representation details, or pass/fail acceptance criteria for the drops.

## pqac-00000015

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt summarizes regulatory expectations for the impact surface in regulatory drop tests (UN/ADR/IMDG referencing ISO 2248): the surface must be horizontal, flat, immovable and unyielding. ISO 2248–referenced criteria include an impact target mass at least 50 times the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤2 mm, rigidity such that deformation does not exceed 0.1 mm under a 10 kg load applied over 100 mm², and sufficient area so the package lands fully on the surface. The text notes a regulatory gap: standards lack guidance on dynamic/transient response, foundation design parameters (e.g., stiffness, eigenfrequencies, stress-wave propagation) and specific design details like concrete pad thickness. It also cites IAEA RAM practice requiring a reinforced concrete foundation with steel plate mass ≥10× specimen and research showing transmitted energy into the target/ground <2%, implying effective unyielding behaviour. The authors pose research questions about whether the 50× mass ratio is the correct metric and whether alternative design parameters could replace it. The excerpt does not provide ASTM D5276 specifics such as required concrete pad thickness, explicit drop heights, payload representation details, or pass/fail acceptance criteria.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

Excerpt describes a guided drop-test setup for filled jerrycans at BAM Test Site. The drop machine is a 14-m high steel frame with a 1000 kg load capacity and an impact area of 2000 x 2000 mm. The foundation is a steel-reinforced concrete block with an anchored steel impact pad weighing 18 000 kg. A custom fixture/harness (slings) secures jerrycans without restraining their deformation; impacts must not be damped. Test procedure controls liquid movement by slow lifting and visual monitoring of the air bubble space to maintain payload position. Only jerrycan body failure was treated as critical; lid or handle failures were not evaluated. Test outcome evaluation used the Bruceton (staircase) method based on the UN Manual of Tests and Criteria. The excerpt provides information relevant to impact surface mass/area, fixture requirements, payload handling, and acceptance/failure definition for these jerrycan tests, but does not specify ASTM D5276 parameters such as concrete pad thickness, prescribed drop heights, or detailed pass/fail criteria used in that ASTM standard.
