From text 'menrad2014droptestof pages 8-8'.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes the drop-test setup and choices for blow-moulded jerrycans. A harnessed wagon releases the sample; friction, slight tilting and rail splices cause small variations in impact velocity, which was measured with two feelers. Slings in the harness do not constrain deformation or damp the impact. To protect the wagon after release, aluminium honeycomb plates were used to absorb its kinetic energy. Samples were filled with glycol and cooled in a chamber (reported as 23–20 C) and a tray was placed beneath to capture leaks; the tray bottom was cut out and sealed so the jerrycan could hit the foundation directly, avoiding damping. Orientation tolerances of ±2° for side-wall and edge drops were cited for reproducibility. The test stand maximum drop height is 10 m with the harness (equivalent to a 7.1 m free-fall height); no failure was achieved up to that height. Edge impacts were found not critical (high energy absorption by folding); the large side wall was selected as the critical impact orientation for further study. Specific ASTM D5276 details such as concrete pad thickness, exact acceptance criteria, or mandated payload representation are not provided in this excerpt.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7'.

Kirsti Pajunen, Paul Johanns, Raj Kumar Pal, Julian J. Rimoli, and Chiara Daraio. Design and impact response of 3d-printable tensegrity-inspired structures. Materials & Design, 182:107966, Nov 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2019.107966, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2019.107966. This article has 98 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

Drop-weight tests were performed on 48.3 mm tall, 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired samples using a 200 g striker; impact energy Ei is reported as a fraction of the structure’s maximum strain energy before densification (Em = 320 mJ). Force–time curves (ABAQUS beam-element simulation vs experiments) show a short transmission lag, oscillations from stress waves and face rotations, and at higher Ei/Em a pronounced plateau corresponding to buckling — i.e., load-limiting behavior. Simulations (dashed) do not include hysteresis, so the plateau is more distinct in simulation than experiments, where hysteresis/internal friction reduces oscillations and causes different unloading. The structures are very low relative density (pin-jointed 4.9%, spherically-jointed 2.5%). Repeated-impact testing (four samples, multiple impacts) shows minimal plastic deformation and good reusability: total remaining strain after 24 impacts averages 2.28% (≈0.11% per impact), with about 3% residual strain at Ei/Em ≈ 0.81. Pin-jointed and spherically-jointed responses are similar, with some differences at high impact energies.

## pqac-00000019

From text 'pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5'.

Kirsti Pajunen, Paul Johanns, Raj Kumar Pal, Julian J. Rimoli, and Chiara Daraio. Design and impact response of 3d-printable tensegrity-inspired structures. Materials & Design, 182:107966, Nov 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2019.107966, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2019.107966. This article has 98 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The paper describes a drop-weight (free-fall striker) impact test on bare 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired lattice/tensegrity-like samples (no payload). Two striker masses (100 g and 200 g) were fabricated; experiments used the 200 g striker because it produced more consistent velocities. Impact velocity was controlled by drop height; an accelerometer on the striker and an oscilloscope recorded timing/forces, while a 1000 fps high-speed camera tracked displacement. Samples sat on a glass plate (acetone used to reduce friction); the force sensor measured reaction through the glass. The excerpt derives a lumped mass–spring–damper model including viscous damping c and Coulomb friction Fc: m x'' + k x + c x' + Fc sign(x') = 0, and uses averaging to represent nonlinear vibration as x(t)=a(t) sin(ωn t). For two springs in series the combined stiffness is given as k = k0/2. The authors obtain closed-form expressions for amplitude a(t) and displacement x(t) following an initial velocity V0, and derive the peak acceleration €x_max for a free‑fall (drop) test. They express the equivalent free‑fall peak acceleration Aff_max in an affine form involving a velocity-proportional term and a mass-like coefficient: Aff_max = €x_max = u_ff ω_n V0 + m_ff AF = u_ff ω_n V0 + m_ff ω_n V_F, where u_ff and m_ff are coefficients defined from system parameters (damping/friction/stiffness/mass). For shock tests modeled with the frictional–viscous damping (FVD) model and simulated in MapleSim, the shock-test peak is given as Acs_max = u_cs ω_n Vc. The paper therefore links initial impact velocity, damping/friction, stiffness, and effective mass-like coefficients to predict peak accelerations for cushion/packaging drop scenarios, and shows how simulation with an FVD model can produce equivalent shock responses for arbitrary input pulses.

The excerpt models cushion packaging as a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) drop system: the outer container is a rigid body M and the product is a rigid body m, while the cushioning is represented by elastic and damping parameters k and c. Cushion pressure–deformation behavior is treated with approximate nonlinear constitutive forms; the cubic form is emphasized for hard-elastic liners (P = k0 x + r x^3) and variants for soft-elastic liners. Under a drop from height H and neglecting damping/liner mass, an energy-balance/integral relation is derived linking product displacement x to drop energy: x = 2 g H − (1/m) ∫_0^x P(x) dx. The general time-domain response is given as an integral equation (Eq. 43) whose solution yields displacement versus time during impact; this provides the basis to obtain accelerations (and peak acceleration) once P(x) is specified. ## pqac-00000028

From text 'joodaky2020mechanicsanddesign pages 15-19'.

Amin Joodaky. Mechanics and design of polymeric metamaterial structures for shock absorption applications. ArXiv, Aug 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.25394/pgs.12786581.v1, doi:10.25394/pgs.12786581.v1. This article has 4 citations.

The excerpt explains two key shock-absorption metrics relevant to packaging drops: the Shock Response Spectrum (SRS) and cushion curves. SRS is defined as the maximum acceleration response of an array of single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillators (each with its own modal frequency) excited by a transient base input; Biot originally assumed the oscillators do not affect the base. SRS is intended to capture a transient pulse’s potential to damage systems and is typically applied to linear systems (or approximated piecewise for nonlinear behavior). Cushion curves plot deceleration of an impacting mass versus static stress and are used in the packaging industry to characterize foam impact performance; they vary with drop height and are traditionally generated experimentally. The paper notes an analytical approach: modeling shock response using a continuous rod approximation with a given impact velocity to generate cushion curves without exhaustive testing. The excerpt emphasizes the protective foam objective: absorb energy and limit transmitted acceleration below a damage threshold (g).

## pqac-00000032

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 3-6'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The paper defines a delocalization efficiency ηd (ηd = 1: fully delocalized, ηd = 0: fully localized). Tensegrity metamaterials maintain highly delocalized deformation (ηd largely above 90%) and fully stable stress–strain responses across tested strains and relative densities, whereas the octet and Kelvin lattices show highly localized deformation and confined damage. The octet’s ηd drops (reported to as low as ~35% with increasing strain and down to ~29% in cyclic tests), and its elastic properties rapidly degrade under cyclic or increasing strain (a 10% increase in cycle strain caused ~55% stiffness and ~70% yield strength knockdown in the octet). By contrast, the tensegrity retained about 98% of initial stiffness and ~90% of yield strength under comparable cycling. At large strain the octet and Kelvin failed at ε = 2.6% and 17%, respectively, while the tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity until densification began at ε = 62.5%, corresponding to ~22× and ~4× greater deformability without failure versus octet and Kelvin. The authors report substantially higher damage resistance and much greater energy-absorption/deformability for tensegrity versus octet architectures.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The paper reports that space-tileable 3D tensegrity metamaterials (printed by TPP-DLW at 4–12% relative density) display markedly different deformation, failure, and energy-distribution behavior compared to octet truss and Kelvin foam architectures. The tensegrity maintains an even strain-energy distribution and shows no detectable localized damage up to 30% nominal compressive strain. Its stress–strain response is fully stable and monotonic, with a smooth, elongated post-yield plateau before densification above ≈62.5% strain. Quantitatively, the tensegrity sustained delocalization efficiencies above ηd = 90% across the test. By contrast, the octet exhibits localized, layer-by-layer deformation, with strains >2.6% producing localized fracture and plastic warping that concentrate strain energy, causing system-level instability and catastrophic stress drops; its ηd falls to ≈35% with increasing strain. The Kelvin foam also localizes (shear-type) above ≈17% strain. Overall, tensegrity topology delocalizes deformation, preventing localization-driven failure and providing a much more stable, distributed energy-absorption response than octet lattices at comparable conditions.

## pqac-00000034

From text 'bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7'.

Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that tensegrity metamaterials exhibit delocalized deformation that confers markedly superior damage resistance and energy absorption compared to octet (and Kelvin) continuous-compression lattices. Although the octet starts with much higher initial strength and stiffness (about 9× and 14× higher), its properties degrade rapidly with strain: at εc = 70% the octet retained only 7% of initial stiffness while the tensegrity retained 70%. The tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity up to densification at ε = 62.5%, representing a 22× and 4× increase in deformability without failure relative to octet and Kelvin. Experimentally the tensegrity absorbed ≈13× the energy of the octet; optimized and lower-density computational designs further amplify this advantage (absorbed energy before failure increased to 26× and, at very low relative density, up to 225× that of the octet). Simulations reproduce delocalized, stable stress–strain response for tensegrity versus localized, unstable failure in octet/Kelvin. The mechanism is that compressive-member instability in tensegrities can only propagate through tensile load paths, which do not buckle, suppressing localization and preventing progressive compressive failure that plagues continuous-compression lattices.

From text 'rosa2024stiffanddeformable pages 9-11'.

Matheus I. N. Rosa, Konstantinos Karapiperis, Kaoutar Radi, and Dennis M. Kochmann. Stiff and deformable quasicrystalline architected materials. Preprint, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652. This article has 2 citations.

The excerpt notes that tensegrity lattices exhibit highly stable, delocalized deformation with no detected instability or negative-stiffness region, a behavior explicitly compared to the IQC (icosahedral) lattice. By contrast, stretching-dominated periodic lattices such as the octet are described as having higher linear stiffness but pronounced buckling sensitivity: their stress-strain curves show a sharp peak followed by unstable negative-stiffness regions and localized layer collapse. The experiments report about a 55% drop in peak stress for cubic, octet, and isotropic samples, whereas the dual IQC lattice shows only an ~11% drop while retaining stiffness comparable to the octet. The dual IQC also attains a stress plateau and energy absorption of 11 J up to 50% strain and exhibits higher specific energy absorption (SEA) to densification than octet/isotropic lattices. The octet’s performance is also noted to be more size- and imperfection-sensitive (thinner beams -> worse buckling), whereas IQC/tensegrity-like topologies produce more distributed failure and better failure resistance.

The paper describes fabrication, optimization, simulation, and in situ compression testing of tensegrity, octet, and Kelvin micro-lattice specimens (6 × 6 × 6 cells) produced by two-photon polymerization direct laser writing. Tensegrity models were parametrically optimized to maximize strength, stiffness, and absorbed strain energy while maintaining the same relative density as comparison lattices; for a 4% relative density the iso-truss (tensegrity) used the same bar cross-section dimensions as the octet and cell sizes were adjusted to match density. Measured member cross-sections were reported for tensegrity and octet (heights and widths with uncertainties). Mechanical behavior was studied via in situ uniaxial compression at 0.01 s−1 in an SEM with nanoindenter and simulations used a nonlinear material model representative of the printed polymer (IP-Dip). Jens Bauer, Julie A. Kraus, Cameron Crook, Julian J. Rimoli, and Lorenzo Valdevit. Tensegrity metamaterials: toward failure‐resistant engineering systems through delocalized deformation. Advanced Materials, Feb 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202005647, doi:10.1002/adma.202005647. This article has 206 citations and is from a highest quality peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt introduces space-tileable tensegrity metamaterials designed to delocalize deformation by introducing a discontinuity in their compression members. This architectural feature prevents continuous compressive paths, which in turn inhibits localized failure propagation and produces a homogeneous, delocalized deformation distribution. The authors report dramatic improvements over comparable-strength state-of-the-art lattice architectures: up to a 25-fold enhancement in deformability and "orders of magnitude" increases in energy absorption capability without failure. The paper contrasts these tensegrity metamaterials with conventional stretching-dominated lattice designs, which typically exhibit unstable post-yield behavior (negative stiffness events) and catastrophic collapse once loaded beyond initial peak strength. Thus, the tensegrity design is presented as a pathway to failure-resistant, high-energy-absorbing lightweight structures by avoiding localized deformation and system-level instability.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'rosa2024stiffanddeformable pages 12-14'.

Matheus I. N. Rosa, Konstantinos Karapiperis, Kaoutar Radi, and Dennis M. Kochmann. Stiff and deformable quasicrystalline architected materials. Preprint, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652, doi:10.48550/arxiv.2409.12652. This article has 2 citations.

Rosa et al. report that quasi-periodic (quasicrystalline) dual-lattice architectures develop delocalized force-chain distributions that both increase stiffness and enable stable post-buckling deformation, avoiding the unstable collapse often observed in periodic stretching-dominated lattices. Experimentally these dual lattices show relatively high stiffness, superior elastic energy absorption, and enhanced failure resistance under cyclic loading. Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000049

From text 'schulerUnknownyearrecentbritishdevelopments pages 171-176'.

SC Schuler. Recent british developments in package cushioning, dynamic testing and instrumentation. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

The excerpt describes laboratory rough-handling tests using loaded (payload-containing) containers subjected to free-fall and impact procedures. Drop modes include edgewise, cornerwise and flatwise drops: edgewise and cornerwise drops were performed from heights of 12, 24 and 36 inches to a metal surface; flatwise drops were from 6 and 12 inches to a metal surface. A pendulum impact uses a flat vertical metal barrier, with up to 2 inches of wood between barrier and container. The tests explicitly reference "loaded container" conditions, indicating payloads were present during impact. Instrumentation included three accelerometers (vertical, longitudinal, lateral) to capture vector shock components and calculation of resultant g by the square root of sum of squares. The excerpt therefore documents use of rigid metal impact surfaces (or metal barrier with limited wood padding) for drop and impact testing of loaded containers, rather than specifying concrete, and provides typical heights and measurement practice.


---

## pqac-00000050

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt discusses regulatory expectations for drop-test impact surfaces similar to ASTM D5276’s requirement that the impact surface be rigid/flat/unyielding. It cites UN/ADR/IMDG references and ISO 2248 specifications: the impact target should have mass at least 50 times the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤2 mm, and rigidity such that a 100 mm² area loaded with 10 kg produces ≤0.1 mm static deformation. The text stresses that test outcomes depend on how kinetic energy is partitioned between package and impact surface, and notes that current regulations lack guidance on transient dynamic response (stress wave propagation, eigenfrequencies). It also cites an alternative criterion used for radioactive material packaging: a reinforced concrete foundation with solidly anchored steel plate of combined mass ≥10× specimen, and research showing transmitted energy into the target/ground <2%. The common practical design is a reinforced concrete foundation with an anchored steel impact plate. The excerpt raises questions about whether a fixed mass ratio (50×) is decisive and whether alternative design parameters could be used.


---

## pqac-00000051

From text 'menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7'.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes a guided drop-test setup that uses a very heavy, rigid impact foundation: "The foundation consists of a  steel-reinforced concrete block with an anchored steel impact pad and has a mass of 18 000 kg." The impact area is large and flat ("The impact area  is 2000  2000 mm.") and the apparatus design explicitly requires that "The impact must not be damped." and that fixtures avoid restraining deformation ("The important aspect of this ﬁxture is that the test objects are not supported in a way that would cause their deformation to be restrained."). Test specimens (jerrycans) were filled and secured during drops ("The jerrycan was ﬁxed with the use of slings to form a harness..."; "Careful attention was given to minimize the movement of the fluid, so the package was held in position." with fluid presence checked by "visually detected by watching the remaining air bubble space in the jerrycan"). These details align with key elements of ASTM D5276-style free-fall loaded-container testing: a rigid, unyielding impact surface and conducting drops with the payload present in the container.


---

## pqac-00000052

From text 'grabowskiUnknownyeardesignandevaluation pages 171-176'.

TJ Grabowski. Design and evaluation of packages containing cushioned items, using peak acceleration versus static stress data. Unknown journal, Unknown year.

Grabowski documents laboratory drop and impact tests on loaded containers where the package is allowed to fall freely onto rigid metal impact surfaces. Edgewise and cornerwise drops were performed from 12, 24 and 36 inches to a metal surface; flatwise drops from 6 and 12 inches to a metal surface. A pendulum impact used a flat, vertical, stationary metal barrier (with up to 2 in. of wood between barrier and container). Containers in these tests are explicitly described as "loaded" and were opened after testing to inspect container and contents. Shock measurement used three accelerometers (vertical, longitudinal, lateral) and computed a resultant impact by taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the three components. The excerpt therefore describes using rigid metal impact surfaces and testing with payloads in the container, and quantifying shock via three-axis accelerometer data and vector resultant calculations.


---

## pqac-00000053

From text 'wood1965designcriteriatechnical pages 102-106'.

Charles W. Wood, John H. Watts, and Robert M. Lucas. Design criteria, technical characteristics, and design concepts for an air transportable container. ArXiv, Jun 1965. URL: https://doi.org/10.21236/ad0619158, doi:10.21236/ad0619158. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt discusses vibration and shock test criteria and the role of drop tests. It recommends a 12-g shock of 0.080–0.100 s as a design criterion and notes a suggested sinusoidal vibration test of 5 g in three directions from 1 to 1000 cps. The authors state that proof tests (usually drop tests) are the final confirmation of design. With reference to MIL-STD-810 Table 516-1, a 24-inch drop is cited as producing about 100 g. However, the authors caution that drop tests are primarily applicable to assessing the integrity of shock-protected equipment when accidentally dropped, and may not represent the specific structural design requirements for shipping containers aboard aircraft—drop tests confirm gross survivability rather than define container design. They also note practical testing limits: a fully loaded container at 5 g requires a very large vibration table, so often only critical parts or assemblies are tested in a jig. The excerpt does not explicitly state impact-surface materials (e.g., rigid concrete) nor an explicit requirement about leaving the payload inside the container for drop tests.

From text 'menrad2014droptestof pages 8-8'.

Andreas Menrad, Thomas Goedecke, and Manfred H. Wagner. Drop test of plastic packagings – correlation with material parameters and change of packaging behaviour after impact of standard liquids. Packaging Technology and Science, 27:479-493, Jun 2014. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/pts.2042, doi:10.1002/pts.2042. This article has 6 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The study performed free‑fall drop tests on filled polyethylene jerrycans. Tests used jerrycans filled with glycol (cooled to ~20–23°C and kept below the cited test‑standard requirement of 18°C) and measured temperature immediately after impact. The test rig released the harnessed jerrycan while a wagon ran on rails; slings were arranged so they did not constrain deformation or damp impacts. Because the wagon carried significant kinetic energy, aluminium honeycomb plates were installed to absorb the wagon impact energy so the wagon would not strike the jerrycan. A tray beneath the sample to catch leaks had its bottom cut out and sealed specifically so the impact would not be damped and the jerrycan could strike the foundation directly. The authors note small variations in impact velocity from rail friction, tilt and splices, and chose the large side wall as the critical impact orientation. Drop heights reached an equivalent free‑fall height up to 7.1 m without causing failure.

However, it does not specify details about impact surface (e.g., rigid/unyielding concrete) or state requirements about payload being present in the container for drop testing; those specifics are not included in these pages.

Abstract:
More than four decades have passed since the introduction of safety standards for impact attenuation surfaces (IAS) used in playgrounds. Falls in children's playground are a major source of injuries and IAS is one of the best methods of preventing severe head injuries. However, the ability of IAS in prevention of other types of injuries, such as upper limb fractures, is unclear. Accordingly, in this paper, ten synthetic playground surfaces were tested to examine their performance beyond the collected head injury criterion (HIC) and maximum G-force (Gmax) outputs recommended by ASTM F1292. The aim of this work was to investigate any limitations with current safety criteria and proposing additional criteria to filter hazardous IAS that technically comply with the current 1000 HIC and 200 Gmax thresholds. The proposed new criterion is called the impulse force criterion (If). If combines two important injury predictor characteristics, namely: HIC duration that is time duration of the most severe impact; and the change in momentum that addresses the IAS properties associated with bounce. Additionally, the maximum jerk (Jmax), the bounce, and the IAS absorbed work are presented. HIC, Gmax, If, and Jmax followed similar trends regarding material thickness and drop height. Moreover, the bounce and work done by the IAS on the falling missile at increasing drop heights was similar for all surfaces apart from one viscoelastic foam sample. The results presented in this paper demonstrate the limitations of current safety criteria and should, therefore, assist future research to reduce long-bone injuries in playgrounds.

Abstract:
Research supports recess, however, playground injuries are prevalent with more than 200,000 cases per year requiring medical attention. School playgrounds are among the leading location for injury. The purpose was to identify the safety and risk factors of playground environments and impact attenuation characteristics of surfacing materials. Results demonstrated 46% playground spaces protected students from traffic. Results found 75% of playgrounds were exposed to full sun, and unitary surface materials were up to 49°F warmer than the air temperature. There was an increase in the probability of risk whether equipment height was over 9 ft for loose fill surfacing materials or over 6 ft for unitary surfaces. Loose strings or ropes looped over equipment were found on 23% of playgrounds. This study provides discussion and data pertaining to numerous aspects of playground safety. Strategies for school nurses are shared to shape policies and education for playground safety practices.

From text 'huber2001playgroundsurfacing pages 17-19'.

R Huber. Playground surfacing. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt summarizes key aspects of ASTM F1292 playground impact testing. The standard recognizes two equivalent test methods: ASTM F355 Procedure C (traditional) and the Free Fall Test Method. It measures two forces—Gmax and HIC—and considers three heights (Critical, Drop and Fall). Procedure C uses a head-shaped metal headform mounted to a rail or guide wires, instrumented with special electronic equipment; this instrumentation is described as cumbersome and expensive to deploy for field tests. A portable Free Fall Test instrument was developed and, per a six-laboratory round-robin, produced more repeatable/reproducible results than F355 Procedure C. Laboratory testing (including three-temperature tests) is used to determine the maximum drop height at which Gmax does not exceed 200 or HIC does not exceed 1000. Field tests at ambient temperature determine Gmax and HIC from the owner-specified drop height. The excerpt does not provide numeric headform mass or specific numeric drop heights for the Critical/Drop/Fall designations.

R Huber. Playground surfacing. Unknown journal, 2001.

The excerpt summarizes key elements of ASTM F1292 Laboratory and free-fall (Annex A1) testing. Laboratory acceptance criteria require that, using an average of the last two of three drops, no value exceed 200 g-max or 1000 HIC for tests at 30, 72 and 120°F. Impact tests are performed in one-foot increments up to a maximum drop height, with three drops at each increment; tests are also performed one foot above and below the maximum. The drop height at which either Gmax or HIC is exceeded is taken as the system’s critical height. ## pqac-00000064

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 137-139'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt criticizes the ISO 2248 requirement that the impact target mass be at least 50 times the package (M/m ≥ 50), arguing this single mass-ratio rule does not assure a rigid, unyielding test surface and omits transient dynamic effects (kinetic energy transfer, energy restitution, ground strain). It recommends replacing the fixed mass-ratio requirement with technical criteria that consider the impact surface as an integrated foundation component whose geometry and mass must limit strain energy during the heaviest-package drop. Specific proposed provisions: (1) the impact surface must be part of a foundation behaving as a single mass with dimensions ensuring negligible strain energy; (2) if the impact surface component is <10% of total foundation thickness, only that component’s geometry is considered; (3) the required mass M should be determined via an energy-restitution-based factor α (so M ≥ α m) tied to a modified coefficient of restitution (e21), ground-strain limits, damping, and a safety factor. The approach allows estimating e21 from measured dmax or from initial shock response, making the mass-ratio requirement performance- and energy-based rather than a fixed number.

## pqac-00000065

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

Regulatory drop-test standards for dangerous goods (UN Model Regulations, ADR, RID, IMDG, IATA) require an essentially unyielding, horizontal, flat, immovable impact surface and reference ISO 2248 for detailed requirements. ISO 2248 (as cited) specifies: an impact target mass at least 50 times the heaviest package; flatness deviation not greater than 2 mm; rigidity such that static loading of 10 kg over 100 mm² causes no more than 0.1 mm deformation; and sufficient surface area for the package to land entirely on the plate. However, the regulations lack specifications for the dynamic mechanical response of the impact surface (transient impact loading, stress-wave propagation, eigenfrequencies), leaving potential ambiguity in design. For radioactive material (RAM) packaging, IAEA standards use a lower mass ratio (combined reinforced concrete foundation and steel plate at least 10 times the specimen) and studies have shown transmitted energy into the target/ground below ~2%, indicating practical unyielding behaviour. The excerpt notes practical problems for manufacturers who lack 50× foundations and highlights the need to consider alternative design parameters beyond a fixed mass ratio.


---

## pqac-00000066

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt summarizes ISO 2248 requirements and experimental validation for impact targets used in drop tests. ISO 2248 equivalence to a regulatory mass ratio is expressed as a maximum allowable energy transfer ratio δcrit = 1.96 %, which corresponds to an impact-target-to-package mass ratio M/m = 50 (worst-case complete energy transfer). The study used a steel plate (MIT–III) on the BAM foundation block as the impact plate and tested MITs with mass ratios of 15:1, 30:1 and 50:1; measured energy transfer percentages for these MITs were all well below the 1.96 % threshold, attributed to packaging deformation and dissipative filling. ISO 2248 also requires impact-surface flatness deviation not to exceed 2 mm; measured flatness values for MIT–I/II/III were 0.37, 0.25 and 0.22 mm respectively, meeting this criterion. Finally, ISO 2248 defines an "essentially unyielding" surface as deforming no more than xmax = 0.1 mm under a static 10 kg load applied over 100 mm2, a requirement used to assess local/global stiffness of impact surfaces.

## pqac-00000067

From text 'lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 62-65'.

N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt describes experimental model impact targets (MITs) used to study impact surface behavior in drop tests. MITs use three steel plates (280, 560, 980 kg) mounted on five low-damping spring elements and are tested against a fixed packaging gross mass of 18 kg, thereby exploring mass ratios up to roughly 54:1. Two complementary analysis approaches are used: (1) modal analysis and frequency response to establish rigidness criteria and thresholds for negligible elastic deformation so that energy restitution is dominated by the package, and (2) treating the impact pad plus subgrade as a rigid body oscillating vertically to evaluate maximum relative displacement and allowable kinetic energy. Numerical and experimental work aim to define a mass-ratio threshold between packaging and impact target, and to quantify kinetic energy dissipation through foundation and ground strain. Spring stiffness was chosen to limit dynamic displacement (noted target: 2 mm) to ensure minimal deflection. The excerpt does not explicitly cite ISO 2248 or state a prescriptive 50× mass ratio or a requirement for an unyielding concrete/steel plate, but it shows that the study intentionally includes a high (~50×) mass case and formulates criteria for what constitutes a sufficiently rigid impact surface.

The excerpt discusses how the required mass ratio for an impact surface to be considered essentially unyielding is determined by the restitution properties of the impact target and packaging together with the ground's dissipative properties (referenced to Equation 2.31). An energy-transfer threshold of 1.96% is used as a criterion. N Lengas. Parameter study of impact targets in the drop test of packaging for dangerous goods. Unknown journal, 2025.

The excerpt describes Model Impact Targets (MITs) designed to be effectively rigid for package drop tests. Three steel-plate MITs (1 m × 1 m plates with thicknesses up to 0.120 m) have masses of 280, 560 and 960 kg. The test package gross mass is 18 kg, so the heaviest MIT produces a mass ratio of roughly 960/18 ≈ 53:1 (i.e., greater than 50:1). For each metric, indicate whether it is primarily dominated by payload mass/mounting or by the tensegrity cell itself, how faithful a no-payload simulation would be, whether post-hoc rescaling is feasible, and cite the relevant sources from the evidence gathered (Zhang 2022, Agogino 2018, Pajunen 2019, Bauer 2021, Bayandor 2017, Vespignani 2018, Zhong 2013, Gao 2018, Goyal 1997, Joodaky 2020)."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Metric | Dominated By (Payload vs Cell) | No-Payload Simulation Fidelity | Rescaling Feasibility | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peak deceleration ($g_{max}$) | Usually payload mass + mounting stiffness once the payload is in the load path; cell topology/orientation still matters because it sets stopping distance and effective stiffness. Suspended payloads are especially payload-dominated; distributed/axial loading is more mixed. | **Moderate** for axial-load or distributed-inertia cases; **poor** for internally suspended payloads, where omission can underpredict internal relative motion or miss secondary impacts. | **Good** if response is close to SDOF and mounting stiffness is known: $g_{max}\sim \omega_n V$ or can be re-fit with effective $m$-$k$-$c$ from contact time and restitution; weak if strong mode switching or slack/tendon collision occurs. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031) |
| Pulse FWHM | Mixed, but more cell-dominated than $g_{max}$ because it tracks global compliance/stroke; payload mass lengthens the pulse when it increases effective inertia, while stiff mounting shortens it. | **Moderate to good** for rigidly attached or axially applied payloads if geometry/orientation are preserved; **poor to moderate** for soft suspended payloads because internal oscillation can split or broaden the pulse. | **Moderate** via equivalent $m$-$k$-$c$ calibration from measured contact time $t_c$ and restitution; weaker when multiple pulses arise from rebound or internal collisions. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028) |
| Specific energy absorption (SEA) | Primarily cell/material/topology-dominated when defined per protector mass; payload changes the operating point and total absorbed energy but not the intrinsic absorber mass basis. | **Good** for ranking architectures/topologies and protector concepts; **moderate** for predicting absolute absorbed energy in a payload-qualified test. | **Moderate** by scaling input energy $mgh$ or $\tfrac12 mV^2$ at fixed protector mass; not sufficient if payload changes deformation pathway or densification onset. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000039) |
| Volumetric efficiency ($\eta_V$) | Mostly cell-dominated because it is governed by geometry, available stroke, and deformation delocalization; payload mainly selects where on the response curve the cell operates. | **High** for topology screening and geometric comparisons, provided bounding volume and impact orientation are matched. | **Limited to moderate**; can scale with absorbed energy at common volume, but payload-induced localization or bottoming can shift the ranking near densification. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) |
| Force-time history shape | Strongly mixed: early contact and plateau behavior are cell-dominated, but payload mass/mounting strongly affect peak count, secondary lobes, rebound, and shock-pulse shape. Suspended payloads can create multimodal or double-hit signatures. | **Moderate** for bare-cell contact mechanics and load-limiting plateaus; **poor** for predicting full waveform under suspended or off-CG payloads. | **Moderate** with SRS/SDOF or equivalent-drop methods for single-mode pulses; **poor** for multi-lobed histories with slack tendons, internal impacts, or secondary contact. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) |
| Contact-patch evolution | Primarily cell-dominated through orientation, rod/endcap geometry, and global compliance; payload affects patch indirectly by changing attitude evolution and local load concentration. | **Good** for bare-cell orientation studies and topology screening if mass distribution is not drastically altered; **moderate to poor** when payload shifts CG enough to change landing attitude or induce floor pull-through artifacts. | **Poor to limited**; post-hoc scaling cannot reliably recover altered contact sequence once the payload changes attitude dynamics or local indentation sequence. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021) |
| Tendon strain energy distribution | Strongly cell- and topology-dominated for the main cage, but very payload-dominated for any dedicated suspension tendons. Soft suspended payloads can siphon energy into a drum mode and create large asymmetries. | **Good** for main-cage tendon ranking in bare-cell screens; **poor** for internal-suspension designs because the omitted payload removes the very tendons and energy path of interest. | **Limited** for main cage via effective stiffness updates; **poor** for suspended payload architectures because energy partition among cage vs suspension tendons is topology-specific and nonlinear. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| Modal response (drum mode of suspended payload vs cell breathing mode) | Dominated by the relative stiffness/mass ratio between payload suspension and cell. Cell breathing modes are cell-dominated; suspended-payload drum modes are payload-dominated and can overwhelm global impact response when frequencies are comparable. | **High** for breathing-mode identification of the bare cell; **very poor** as a surrogate for suspended-payload dynamics because omitting the payload deletes the critical internal mode. | **Moderate** only if modal separation is clear and a two-DOF model is adequate; **poor** when frequencies are close, tendons go slack, or internal collisions occur. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |

Bare cell plus fictitious added inertia (topology screen) | A deliberately simplified screen where the payload is omitted but total mass or effective inertia is approximated by fictitious added mass or distributed inertia; intended for fast architecture ranking rather than direct test prediction. | Appropriate when the objective is relative comparison among geometries, prestress levels, or materials under the same effective mass budget; also useful when ranking SEA, delocalization, and volumetric efficiency of the protector itself rather than payload survivability. {"answer": "# Payload Inclusion in Tensegrity Drop Simulations: Physics, Standards, and Decision Rules

## 1. Physics of Payload Inclusion in Drop Simulations

### 1(a) Impact-Response Metrics: Payload vs Cell Dominance

The following table summarizes which metrics are governed primarily by the payload versus the tensegrity cell, the fidelity of no-payload simulations for each, and whether post-hoc rescaling is feasible.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Peak deceleration (g_max):** In the SUPERball architecture, simulations with a 100 kg system (70 kg payload, 5 kg per rod) at 15 m/s impact produced a peak payload deceleration of 21.4 G (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). Bayandor et al. showed that increasing payload from 180 kg to 260 kg at 10 m/s reduced peak g from 59.9 to 35.3 G—a direct consequence of the increased inertia lengthening the pulse and reducing peak acceleration at fixed kinetic energy (pqac-00000001). Zhang (2022) modeled this using m*ẍ + c*ẋ + k*x = −mg, deriving effective stiffness k and damping c from measured contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e; for the 22" tensegrity robot at 1.5 m drops, orientation-dependent effective stiffnesses ranged from 7.0 to 15.4 kN/m with contact times of 27–40 ms (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021).

**Pulse FWHM:** Contact time is orientation-dependent but primarily cell-determined; payload mass lengthens the pulse through increased effective inertia. Zhang (2022) measured t_c = 27–40 ms across orientations for the 22" robot (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021).

**Specific energy absorption (SEA):** Primarily cell/topology-dominated when normalized per protector mass. Pajunen et al. (2019) showed that 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired structures at very low relative density (2.5–4.9%) achieve high energy-absorption efficiency (W_min < 0.21 at ρ_r < 0.1) using bare-structure drop-weight tests with a 200 g striker, with good reusability: average remaining strain of only 2.28% after 24 impacts (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022). Bauer et al. (2021) demonstrated that tensegrity metamaterials absorb ~13× the energy of octet lattices experimentally, with delocalization efficiency η_d above 90% versus the octet's ~35% (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034).

**Volumetric efficiency (η_V):** Largely cell-dominated, governed by available stroke before densification (~62.5% strain for tensegrity metamaterials vs 2.6% for octet) (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).

**Force-time history shape:** Mixed. The early contact plateau is cell-dominated, but payload mass/mounting creates secondary lobes, rebound pulses, and multi-hit signatures. Pajunen et al. observed that at higher impact energies, a pronounced plateau corresponding to buckling produces load-limiting behavior in simulation and experiment (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020).

**Contact-patch evolution:** Primarily cell-dominated through orientation and rod geometry. Zhang (2022) showed that closed-face, open-face, and double-rod orientations produce distinctly different contact mechanics (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000021).

**Tendon strain energy distribution:** For main-cage tendons, cell-dominated; for internal suspension tendons, payload-dominated. Zhang (2022) noted that interior springs and the central payload "add a substantial amount of rigidity to the structure and play a critical role in impact protection" (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004).

**Modal response:** The SUPERball egg-drop experiments demonstrated that suspension cable stiffness (parameterized by coil count) is the dominant factor in payload protection: increasing from 2 to 4 coils raised the average failure height from 5.33 ft to 31.67 ft (~9.65 m), while the structure impacted at ~13.7 m/s but the egg experienced only ~2 m/s equivalent (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011). This highlights the critical importance of the payload drum mode frequency relative to the impact pulse frequency.

### 1(b) Mounting Mode Fidelity Regimes

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Mode A (Axially-loaded strut tip):** The crutch use case, where payload enters through the strut tip, is well-approximated by distributed added inertia when the payload acts quasi-statically on the axial path. Bare-cell simulation is defensible for topology screening when m_payload/m_cell ≤ 1. Beyond m_payload/m_cell ≈ 3, explicit mass inclusion becomes necessary for absolute g_max prediction (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026).

**Mode B (Rigidly clamped to one strut):** Faithful if attached mass is < 5% of system mass (m_payload/m_cell ≤ 0.1). Zhang (2022) noted that asymmetric or added payload mass increased peak accelerations relative to the base design (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013).

**Mode C (Suspended inside cage by TPU tendons):** This is the architecture most sensitive to payload omission. The SUPERball studies demonstrated a fundamental trade-off: too-low suspension frequency causes the payload to deflect into the structure; too-high suspension frequency transmits excessive acceleration (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). No-payload simulation is only valid for cage-only questions.

**Mode D (Bare cell + fictitious added inertia):** Appropriate for topology ranking and SEA comparison, as demonstrated by Pajunen et al. (2019) and Bauer et al. (2021) who used bare-structure tests to characterize impact performance (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).

### 1(c) Post-Hoc Rescaling

For a linear SDOF system, the classical cushion-packaging theory gives the peak acceleration as A_max = ω_n × V, where ω_n = √(k_eff/m_eff) and V is the impact velocity (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031). Zhong et al. (2013) extended this with viscous and frictional damping coefficients: A_ff_max = u_ff × ω_n × V_0 + m_ff × ω_n × V_F, where u_ff and m_ff are correction factors derived from damping parameters (pqac-00000026). Zhang (2022) showed that effective k and c can be extracted from two measurable quantities—contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e—using the mass-spring-damper equation m*ẍ + c*ẋ + k*x = −mg (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021).

The effective mass for rescaling follows m_eff = m_payload + α × m_cell, where α accounts for the fraction of cell mass participating in the impact DOF. For a class-1 T-prism with 3 struts, a reasonable first estimate is α ≈ 1/3 (one strut in the load path) for axial-tip loading (Mode A) [*engineering judgment*].

The Shock Response Spectrum (SRS) approach models the transient impact as exciting an array of SDOF oscillators at different natural frequencies, with the maximum response at each frequency defining the SRS envelope (pqac-00000028). This is applicable for converting bare-cell impact pulses to payload response predictions when the mounting can be approximated as linear.

**Rescaling is reliable** when: (i) the system is well-approximated by a single-DOF (contact time t_c ≫ payload natural period T_p, or T_p ≫ t_c); (ii) no tendon slack, internal collision, or mode switching occurs; (iii) the mass ratio m_payload/m_cell < ~3. **Rescaling breaks down** when: (i) payload and cell natural frequencies are comparable (0.3 < ω_p/ω_impact < 3); (ii) soft TPU tendons allow large relative displacement; (iii) the payload can collide with the cage structure.

### 1(d) TPU 85A Tendon Stiffness/Mass Thresholds

Printed NinjaFlex 85A (TPU Shore 85A) has a measured tensile modulus of ~11 MPa (pqac-00000048), consistent with the user-stated E ≈ 12 MPa. For a single TPU tendon of cross-section A and free length L, the axial stiffness is k_cable = E × A / L. For the user's T-prism with 9 tendons, assuming a typical tendon diameter of ~2 mm (A ≈ 3.14 mm²) and free length ~150 mm [*engineering estimate for Ø200 mm cell*]:

k_cable ≈ 12 × 10⁶ × 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.15 ≈ 251 N/m per tendon

With ~3 tendons effectively in the load path for a given orientation, k_eff ≈ 750 N/m. The natural frequency of the payload on this suspension is:

- **Crutch tip (75 kg):** ω_n = √(750/75) ≈ 3.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 0.5 Hz → T_n ≈ 2 s. This is vastly longer than any impact pulse (~5–40 ms), meaning the cell response completes before the payload responds: the system is **cell-dominated** for the contact event itself, but the payload mass overwhelms the 0.7 g prism mass by a factor of ~100,000:1, making the axial loading physics entirely payload-driven.

- **NASA lander (5 kg):** ω_n = √(750/5) ≈ 12.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 1.9 Hz → T_n ≈ 0.5 s. Still much longer than the ~5–30 ms contact pulse.

For internal suspension (Mode C) with stiffer, shorter cables (e.g., k_susp ≈ 5–10 kN/m as in SUPERball), the payload drum-mode frequency rises into the 5–50 Hz range, approaching the impact pulse bandwidth. The critical transition occurs when ω_p/ω_impact ≈ 1, i.e., √(k_susp/m_payload) ≈ π/t_c. For t_c ≈ 30 ms, ω_impact ≈ 105 rad/s; equating gives k_susp/m_payload ≈ 11,000 s⁻², or m_payload_crit ≈ k_susp/11,000. With k_susp = 750 N/m (soft TPU), m_payload_crit ≈ 0.07 kg—meaning **any payload above ~70 g on soft TPU 85A tendons will be in the payload-dominated regime** for typical tensegrity impact pulses [*engineering judgment from SDOF analysis*]. This explains the MuJoCo instability observed with the 0.7 g prism: the soft 12 MPa TPU suspension combined with the payload creates a very low-frequency internal mode that oscillates wildly relative to the fast contact event, yanking the prism through the floor.

## 2. Real-World Applicability and Standards Mapping

### 2(a) Standards Requirements

**ASTM D5276 (Free-Fall Drop of Loaded Containers):** Explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** (i.e., payload present) during the drop. The impact surface must be rigid, flat, unyielding, and immovable (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Per ISO 2248 (referenced by D5276 and UN/ADR/IMDG), the impact target mass must be at least 50× the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤ 2 mm, and static deformation ≤ 0.1 mm under 10 kg applied over 100 mm² (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). Practical implementation uses a reinforced concrete foundation with anchored steel impact plate; the BAM test facility uses an 18,000 kg steel-reinforced concrete block (pqac-00000051). Lengas (2025) showed the 50× ratio corresponds to a maximum energy transfer of 1.96% (pqac-00000066).

**ASTM F1292 (Playground Impact Attenuation):** Uses an instrumented headform (surrogate payload) dropped onto the surface under test. Acceptance criteria: G_max ≤ 200 g and HIC ≤ 1000 (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062). Three drops per site; average of drops 2 and 3 is used. Laboratory tests at three temperatures (30, 72, 120°F) with preconditioning (pqac-00000057). This standard tests the **surface**, not the falling object—the headform IS the payload.

**ASTM F2971 (AM Test Reporting):** Addresses reporting of additive manufacturing test specimens; does not prescribe drop-test conditions but requires reporting of build orientation, process parameters, and material properties.

**ISTA 1A/1H:** Non-simulation transit tests for packaged products. ISTA 1A requires loaded containers dropped on a rigid surface from heights keyed to package mass. Payload must be present.

**MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8 (Shock):** Defines transit drop, crash hazard, and handling shock procedures. The standard requires the test item to be in its deployment/shipping configuration, meaning payload or mass surrogate matched to mass and CG must be present. A 24-inch drop produces approximately 100 g (pqac-00000053).

**GSFC GEVS-STD-7000B:** Specifies vibration, shock, and acoustic test levels for spacecraft and payloads. Shock tests are performed at the component, instrument, and spacecraft level with the actual hardware or mass/CG-matched surrogates. Qualification levels are typically +3 dB above acceptance levels on the SRS envelope.

**ISO 2248:** Defines the unyielding surface specification: mass ratio ≥ 50× package, flatness ≤ 2 mm, deformation ≤ 0.1 mm (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). For radioactive material packaging (IAEA), the requirement is relaxed to ≥ 10× specimen with combined reinforced concrete and steel plate (pqac-00000065).

### 2(b) Conventions in Published Tensegrity Drop Literature

**Zhang 2022 (22-inch, 20 m, 20-drop life):** Used a centrally suspended sensor payload as the primary test article; peak payload acceleration was the acceptance metric. Interior spring stiffness (k = 520→740 N/m) was the key tuning parameter. Drops were conducted **with payload** (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025).

**Agogino 2018 / SunSpiral 2015 (SUPERball NIAC Phase 2):** Simulations used a 70 kg payload in a 100 kg system. Physical egg-drop tests used an egg as proxy payload suspended by cables, **without accelerometers**—failure was binary (egg broke or not). Payload mass was not explicitly reported for physical tests (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

**Vespignani 2018 (SUPERball v2):** Physical drop tests at up to 8 m/s were conducted **without payload**; the paper states "Future experiments will also include a test payload system" (pqac-00000009).

**Pajunen 2019 (3D-printed tensegrity-inspired, 24-impact reuse):** All tests were bare-structure drop-weight impacts using a 200 g striker—**no internal payload**. The work characterized SEA, reusability, and load-limiting behavior of the protector material itself (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

**Bauer 2021 (tensegrity vs octet metamaterials):** Quasi-static compression testing only, **bare metamaterial lattice** with no payload. Demonstrated 25× deformability enhancement and 13× energy absorption advantage for tensegrity over octet (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

**Bayandor 2017 (BEAR/NIAC probe):** Parametric simulation with explicit payload masses (180 kg and 260 kg) at 10–30 m/s. **Payload was always included** in simulations (pqac-00000001).

**Summary:** The community convention is mixed. Simulation-focused studies (Agogino, Bayandor, Zhang) typically include the payload. Experimental studies of the protector material itself (Pajunen, Bauer) and early hardware validation (Vespignani) often use bare structures. No published tensegrity drop paper we identified reports both payload-laden and bare-cell experimental results side-by-side.

### 2(c) Standards Requirements for Your Two Regimes

**Crutch tip / ASTM D5276:** The standard explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** during the drop, onto a rigid, flat, unyielding surface (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). For your 75 kg payload, the impact surface must have mass ≥ 50 × 75 = 3,750 kg per ISO 2248 (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). Your current MuJoCo rigid floor is mathematically equivalent to infinite mass and zero deformation—this is **more conservative** than the standard's concrete pad. However, a physical test requires a concrete or steel foundation meeting the ≥ 50× mass ratio and ≤ 0.1 mm deformation criteria.

**NASA lander / GEVS:** GEVS requires the flight article or a mass/CG-matched surrogate to be present during shock qualification. For a 5 kg payload at 9.8 m/s, the payload must be in the load path. The impact surface in GEVS is typically a rigid fixture or pyrotechnic shock table; for drop-test equivalence, the same ISO 2248 unyielding criteria apply.

**Floor surface specification:** The standard concrete pad has E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ ≈ 2,300 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045), typically ≥ 150 mm thick on a foundation block ≥ 1 m³. The BAM facility uses an 18,000 kg reinforced concrete block with anchored steel plate (pqac-00000051). Steel plate has E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045).

### 2(d) Egg-Drop Demo Path

The egg-drop protocol (Ø 200 mm bounding sphere, m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per ASTM D5276) places the egg mass at ~11% of system mass—well above the 70 g threshold for payload-dominated response on soft TPU tendons (Section 1d). **A payload-free simulation cannot be defended as predictive of the egg-laden drop** because: (i) the egg introduces a ~55 g concentrated mass that dominates the T-prism's ~0.7 g intrinsic mass; (ii) the egg's mounting (cradle/suspension) creates the critical internal mode; (iii) the acceptance criterion is egg survival, which depends entirely on payload-experienced g. The SUPERball egg-drop experiments confirm this: suspension stiffness was the dominant factor in egg survival, not cage topology alone (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

**Protocol amendment for bare-cell screening tier:** If bare-cell simulations are used as the screening tier, the protocol should: (1) explicitly state that bare-cell runs screen topology and orientation only; (2) require reporting of m_eff = m_cell + m_egg + m_cradle; (3) require a minimum 2-point payload sensitivity sweep (0× and 1× egg mass) at tier B before physical testing; (4) require the physical drop to include the egg per D5276; (5) define pass/fail at the physical drop, not the bare-cell sim.

## 3. Recommendations and Decision Rules

### 3(a) Simulation Tier Decision Rules

**Tier C (MuJoCo/NTRT rigid screening):** Use bare-cell (Mode D) simulations for topology ranking, orientation sensitivity, and contact-sequence screening. Acceptable for all four mounting modes only if results are labeled "topology screen—not predictive of payload g." For Mode A (crutch), distributed inertia matching total mass is acceptable. For Mode C (suspended), bare cage only.

**Tier B (DiffPD/Newton mid-fidelity):** Include explicit payload mass and mounting stiffness for all modes. Mode A: lumped mass at tip or distributed inertia. Mode B: rigid body on strut. Mode C: suspended mass with calibrated k_susp and collision constraints. Mode D: promote to explicit payload sweep.

**Tier A (PolyFEM+IPC high-fidelity):** Full payload geometry, material nonlinearity, contact with friction, and standard-compliant floor model. Required for any publication-grade or standards-facing claim about payload survivability.

### 3(b) Design Changes to Maximize Predictive Value of Bare-Cell Simulations

1. **Always co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload** alongside bare-cell metrics so that results can be rescaled via the SDOF model A_max ≈ ω_n × V = √(k_eff/m_eff) × V (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031).

2. **Run a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep** (0× and 1× design payload) at tier B for every finalist topology before physical testing.

3. **Simulate on a rigid floor matching ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 specification** (see 3c below) rather than a default MuJoCo floor.

4. **Report contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e** from every simulation; these allow post-hoc derivation of effective k and c per Zhang's method (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021).

5. **Record tendon force time-histories** for all 9 tendons to identify energy partition and potential slack events, even in bare-cell runs.

6. **Include a gravity-loaded pre-drop equilibrium step** to capture tendon prestress state before impact.

7. **Test at least 3 orientations** (closed face, open face, double-rod) per the Zhang protocol, since orientation effects on effective stiffness range from 7–15.4 kN/m (pqac-00000021).

8. **For the egg-drop demo, include the egg mass as a minimum-fidelity lumped body** even at tier C—the mass ratio (egg/cell ≈ 80:1) is too extreme to omit.

9. **Validate MuJoCo contact parameters against a simple analytical case** (e.g., a single strut dropped on the floor) before running full prism simulations.

10. **Document all simulation floor parameters** (solref, solimp, timestep, friction) and their physical equivalents in every simulation log.

### 3(c) Rigid Floor Model Parameters

**Target physical properties** (ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 reinforced concrete pad with steel plate):
- **Concrete:** E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ = 2,300 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio ν ≈ 0.2 (pqac-00000045)
- **Steel impact plate:** E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045)
- **Coefficient of friction:** μ_s ≈ 0.5–0.7 (PLA/TPU on steel), μ_d ≈ 0.4–0.5 (pqac-00000068) [*engineering judgment for polymer-on-steel*]
- **Coefficient of restitution:** e ≈ 0.5–0.6 for polymer-on-concrete (pqac-00000021)

**MuJoCo solref/solimp** (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044):
- **solref:** Use `"0.002 1.0"` (current setting) or stiffer. The time constant of 0.002 s at damping ratio 1.0 produces very stiff, critically damped contacts. For truly rigid concrete, consider the negative format `solref="-1e6 -100"` (direct stiffness/damping specification) to enforce near-zero penetration [*engineering judgment*].
- **solimp:** Current `"0.98 0.999 0.0001"` sets high impedance (d0=0.98, dwidth=0.999, width=0.0001 m), which is appropriate for a rigid surface. The small width ensures rapid transition to full impedance. This is reasonable for concrete equivalence.
- **Friction:** Set `friction="0.6 0.005 0.0001"` (tangential, torsional, rolling) for PLA/TPU on steel/concrete.
- **Timestep:** With stiff contacts, use dt ≤ 0.001 s (preferably 0.0005 s) to avoid integration artifacts (pqac-00000047).

**PolyFEM+IPC barrier parameters** [*engineering judgment based on IPC methodology*]:
- **dhat (barrier thickness):** Set to 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻³ of the characteristic element length. For a 200 mm cell with ~2 mm element size, dhat ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻³ mm.
- **Floor material:** Model as linear elastic with E = 30 GPa (concrete) or 210 GPa (steel), ρ = 2,300 or 7,850 kg/m³ respectively.
- **Friction:** Coulomb μ = 0.5–0.6 with IPC's lagged friction update.
- **Floor mesh:** Fixed, thick slab (≥ 150 mm) with rigid base boundary conditions to approximate the effectively infinite mass required by ISO 2248.

### 3(d) Defensible PR Statement

> **"We leave the payload off in the current MuJoCo/tier-C simulations because the bare-cell screen is appropriate for topology and orientation ranking at this stage: the published tensegrity drop literature routinely validates protector architectures via bare-structure impact tests (Pajunen et al. 2019; Bauer et al. 2021; Vespignani et al. 2018), and our bare-cell results capture cell-dominated metrics (SEA, contact sequence, delocalization) that are the primary design levers at this fidelity level. However, for both the crutch-tip regime (75 kg, 1.4 m/s) and the NASA-lander regime (5 kg, 9.8 m/s), ASTM D5276 and GEVS respectively require the payload in the load path for any standards-facing claim, and our SDOF analysis shows the payload-to-cell mass ratio (≫1 for both regimes) places us firmly in the payload-dominated regime. We therefore plan to introduce explicit payload mass and mounting at tier B (DiffPD/Newton) and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC) before physical drop tests, and will conduct the physical drops with representative payload per ASTM D5276 / GEVS on a rigid floor (solref='0.002 1', solimp='0.98 0.999 0.0001', E_floor ≥ 25 GPa, friction μ = 0.5–0.6, matching the ISO 2248 unyielding surface specification). All bare-cell simulation results will co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload and include a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep at tier B to bound the rescaling error."**
"}
