The SUPERball studies demonstrated a fundamental trade-off: too-low suspension frequency causes the payload to deflect into the structure; too-high suspension frequency transmits excessive acceleration (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008). No-payload simulation is only valid for cage-only questions.

**Mode D (Bare cell + fictitious added inertia):** Appropriate for topology ranking and SEA comparison, as demonstrated by Pajunen et al. (2019) and Bauer et al. (2021) who used bare-structure tests to characterize impact performance (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).

### 1(c) Post-Hoc Rescaling

For a linear SDOF system, the classical cushion-packaging theory gives the peak acceleration as A_max = ω_n × V, where ω_n = √(k_eff/m_eff) and V is the impact velocity (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031). Zhong et al. (2013) extended this with viscous and frictional damping coefficients: A_ff_max = u_ff × ω_n × V_0 + m_ff × ω_n × V_F, where u_ff and m_ff are correction factors derived from damping parameters (pqac-00000026). Zhang (2022) showed that effective k and c can be extracted from two measurable quantities—contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e—using the mass-spring-damper equation m*ẍ + c*ẋ + k*x = −mg (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021).

The effective mass for rescaling follows m_eff = m_payload + α × m_cell, where α accounts for the fraction of cell mass participating in the impact DOF. For a class-1 T-prism with 3 struts, a reasonable first estimate is α ≈ 1/3 (one strut in the load path) for axial-tip loading (Mode A) [*engineering judgment*].

The Shock Response Spectrum (SRS) approach models the transient impact as exciting an array of SDOF oscillators at different natural frequencies, with the maximum response at each frequency defining the SRS envelope (pqac-00000028). This is applicable for converting bare-cell impact pulses to payload response predictions when the mounting can be approximated as linear.

**Rescaling is reliable** when: (i) the system is well-approximated by a single-DOF (contact time t_c ≫ payload natural period T_p, or T_p ≫ t_c); (ii) no tendon slack, internal collision, or mode switching occurs; (iii) the mass ratio m_payload/m_cell < ~3. **Rescaling breaks down** when: (i) payload and cell natural frequencies are comparable (0.3 < ω_p/ω_impact < 3); (ii) soft TPU tendons allow large relative displacement; (iii) the payload can collide with the cage structure.

### 1(d) TPU 85A Tendon Stiffness/Mass Thresholds

Printed NinjaFlex 85A (TPU Shore 85A) has a measured tensile modulus of ~11 MPa (pqac-00000048), consistent with the user-stated E ≈ 12 MPa. For a single TPU tendon of cross-section A and free length L, the axial stiffness is k_cable = E × A / L. For the user's T-prism with 9 tendons, assuming a typical tendon diameter of ~2 mm (A ≈ 3.14 mm²) and free length ~150 mm [*engineering estimate for Ø200 mm cell*]:

k_cable ≈ 12 × 10⁶ × 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.15 ≈ 251 N/m per tendon

With ~3 tendons effectively in the load path for a given orientation, k_eff ≈ 750 N/m. The natural frequency of the payload on this suspension is:

- **Crutch tip (75 kg):** ω_n = √(750/75) ≈ 3.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 0.5 Hz → T_n ≈ 2 s. This is vastly longer than any impact pulse (~5–40 ms), meaning the cell response completes before the payload responds: the system is **cell-dominated** for the contact event itself, but the payload mass overwhelms the 0.7 g prism mass by a factor of ~100,000:1, making the axial loading physics entirely payload-driven.

- **NASA lander (5 kg):** ω_n = √(750/5) ≈ 12.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 1.9 Hz → T_n ≈ 0.5 s. Still much longer than the ~5–30 ms contact pulse.

For internal suspension (Mode C) with stiffer, shorter cables (e.g., k_susp ≈ 5–10 kN/m as in SUPERball), the payload drum-mode frequency rises into the 5–50 Hz range, approaching the impact pulse bandwidth. The critical transition occurs when ω_p/ω_impact ≈ 1, i.e., √(k_susp/m_payload) ≈ π/t_c. For t_c ≈ 30 ms, ω_impact ≈ 105 rad/s; equating gives k_susp/m_payload ≈ 11,000 s⁻², or m_payload_crit ≈ k_susp/11,000. With k_susp = 750 N/m (soft TPU), m_payload_crit ≈ 0.07 kg—meaning **any payload above ~70 g on soft TPU 85A tendons will be in the payload-dominated regime** for typical tensegrity impact pulses [*engineering judgment from SDOF analysis*]. This explains the MuJoCo instability observed with the 0.7 g prism: the soft 12 MPa TPU suspension combined with the payload creates a very low-frequency internal mode that oscillates wildly relative to the fast contact event, yanking the prism through the floor.

## 2. Real-World Applicability and Standards Mapping

### 2(a) Standards Requirements

**ASTM D5276 (Free-Fall Drop of Loaded Containers):** Explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** (i.e., payload present) during the drop. The impact surface must be rigid, flat, unyielding, and immovable (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). Per ISO 2248 (referenced by D5276 and UN/ADR/IMDG), the impact target mass must be at least 50× the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤ 2 mm, and static deformation ≤ 0.1 mm under 10 kg applied over 100 mm² (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). Practical implementation uses a reinforced concrete foundation with anchored steel impact plate; the BAM test facility uses an 18,000 kg steel-reinforced concrete block (pqac-00000051). Lengas (2025) showed the 50× ratio corresponds to a maximum energy transfer of 1.96% (pqac-00000066).

**ASTM F1292 (Playground Impact Attenuation):** Uses an instrumented headform (surrogate payload) dropped onto the surface under test. Acceptance criteria: G_max ≤ 200 g and HIC ≤ 1000 (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062). Three drops per site; average of drops 2 and 3 is used. Laboratory tests at three temperatures (30, 72, 120°F) with preconditioning (pqac-00000057). This standard tests the **surface**, not the falling object—the headform IS the payload.

**ASTM F2971 (AM Test Reporting):** Addresses reporting of additive manufacturing test specimens; does not prescribe drop-test conditions but requires reporting of build orientation, process parameters, and material properties.

**ISTA 1A/1H:** Non-simulation transit tests for packaged products. ISTA 1A requires loaded containers dropped on a rigid surface from heights keyed to package mass. Payload must be present.

**MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8 (Shock):** Defines transit drop, crash hazard, and handling shock procedures. The standard requires the test item to be in its deployment/shipping configuration, meaning payload or mass surrogate matched to mass and CG must be present. A 24-inch drop produces approximately 100 g (pqac-00000053).

**GSFC GEVS-STD-7000B:** Specifies vibration, shock, and acoustic test levels for spacecraft and payloads. Shock tests are performed at the component, instrument, and spacecraft level with the actual hardware or mass/CG-matched surrogates. Qualification levels are typically +3 dB above acceptance levels on the SRS envelope.

**ISO 2248:** Defines the unyielding surface specification: mass ratio ≥ 50× package, flatness ≤ 2 mm, deformation ≤ 0.1 mm (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). For radioactive material packaging (IAEA), the requirement is relaxed to ≥ 10× specimen with combined reinforced concrete and steel plate (pqac-00000065).

### 2(b) Conventions in Published Tensegrity Drop Literature

**Zhang 2022 (22-inch, 20 m, 20-drop life):** Used a centrally suspended sensor payload as the primary test article; peak payload acceleration was the acceptance metric. Interior spring stiffness (k = 520→740 N/m) was the key tuning parameter. Drops were conducted **with payload** (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025).

**Agogino 2018 / SunSpiral 2015 (SUPERball NIAC Phase 2):** Simulations used a 70 kg payload in a 100 kg system. Physical egg-drop tests used an egg as proxy payload suspended by cables, **without accelerometers**—failure was binary (egg broke or not). Payload mass was not explicitly reported for physical tests (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

**Vespignani 2018 (SUPERball v2):** Physical drop tests at up to 8 m/s were conducted **without payload**; the paper states "Future experiments will also include a test payload system" (pqac-00000009).

**Pajunen 2019 (3D-printed tensegrity-inspired, 24-impact reuse):** All tests were bare-structure drop-weight impacts using a 200 g striker—**no internal payload**. The work characterized SEA, reusability, and load-limiting behavior of the protector material itself (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024).

**Bauer 2021 (tensegrity vs octet metamaterials):** Quasi-static compression testing only, **bare metamaterial lattice** with no payload. Demonstrated 25× deformability enhancement and 13× energy absorption advantage for tensegrity over octet (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037).

**Bayandor 2017 (BEAR/NIAC probe):** Parametric simulation with explicit payload masses (180 kg and 260 kg) at 10–30 m/s. **Payload was always included** in simulations (pqac-00000001).

**Summary:** The community convention is mixed. Simulation-focused studies (Agogino, Bayandor, Zhang) typically include the payload. Experimental studies of the protector material itself (Pajunen, Bauer) and early hardware validation (Vespignani) often use bare structures. No published tensegrity drop paper we identified reports both payload-laden and bare-cell experimental results side-by-side.

### 2(c) Standards Requirements for Your Two Regimes

**Crutch tip / ASTM D5276:** The standard explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** during the drop, onto a rigid, flat, unyielding surface (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). For your 75 kg payload, the impact surface must have mass ≥ 50 × 75 = 3,750 kg per ISO 2248 (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000066). Your current MuJoCo rigid floor is mathematically equivalent to infinite mass and zero deformation—this is **more conservative** than the standard's concrete pad. However, a physical test requires a concrete or steel foundation meeting the ≥ 50× mass ratio and ≤ 0.1 mm deformation criteria.

**NASA lander / GEVS:** GEVS requires the flight article or a mass/CG-matched surrogate to be present during shock qualification. For a 5 kg payload at 9.8 m/s, the payload must be in the load path. The impact surface in GEVS is typically a rigid fixture or pyrotechnic shock table; for drop-test equivalence, the same ISO 2248 unyielding criteria apply.

**Floor surface specification:** The standard concrete pad has E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ ≈ 2,300 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045), typically ≥ 150 mm thick on a foundation block ≥ 1 m³. The BAM facility uses an 18,000 kg reinforced concrete block with anchored steel plate (pqac-00000051). Steel plate has E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045).

### 2(d) Egg-Drop Demo Path

The egg-drop protocol (Ø 200 mm bounding sphere, m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per ASTM D5276) places the egg mass at ~11% of system mass—well above the 70 g threshold for payload-dominated response on soft TPU tendons (Section 1d). **A payload-free simulation cannot be defended as predictive of the egg-laden drop** because: (i) the egg introduces a ~55 g concentrated mass that dominates the T-prism's ~0.7 g intrinsic mass; (ii) the egg's mounting (cradle/suspension) creates the critical internal mode; (iii) the acceptance criterion is egg survival, which depends entirely on payload-experienced g. The SUPERball egg-drop experiments confirm this: suspension stiffness was the dominant factor in egg survival, not cage topology alone (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011).

**Protocol amendment for bare-cell screening tier:** If bare-cell simulations are used as the screening tier, the protocol should: (1) explicitly state that bare-cell runs screen topology and orientation only; (2) require reporting of m_eff = m_cell + m_egg + m_cradle; (3) require a minimum 2-point payload sensitivity sweep (0× and 1× egg mass) at tier B before physical testing; (4) require the physical drop to include the egg per D5276; (5) define pass/fail at the physical drop, not the bare-cell sim.

## 3. Recommendations and Decision Rules

### 3(a) Simulation Tier Decision Rules

**Tier C (MuJoCo/NTRT rigid screening):** Use bare-cell (Mode D) simulations for topology ranking, orientation sensitivity, and contact-sequence screening. Acceptable for all four mounting modes only if results are labeled "topology screen—not predictive of payload g." For Mode A (crutch), distributed inertia matching total mass is acceptable. For Mode C (suspended), bare cage only.

**Tier B (DiffPD/Newton mid-fidelity):** Include explicit payload mass and mounting stiffness for all modes. Mode A: lumped mass at tip or distributed inertia. Mode B: rigid body on strut. Mode C: suspended mass with calibrated k_susp and collision constraints. Mode D: promote to explicit payload sweep.

**Tier A (PolyFEM+IPC high-fidelity):** Full payload geometry, material nonlinearity, contact with friction, and standard-compliant floor model. Required for any publication-grade or standards-facing claim about payload survivability.

### 3(b) Design Changes to Maximize Predictive Value of Bare-Cell Simulations

1. **Always co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload** alongside bare-cell metrics so that results can be rescaled via the SDOF model A_max ≈ ω_n × V = √(k_eff/m_eff) × V (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031).

2. **Run a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep** (0× and 1× design payload) at tier B for every finalist topology before physical testing.

3. **Simulate on a rigid floor matching ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 specification** (see 3c below) rather than a default MuJoCo floor.

4. **Report contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e** from every simulation; these allow post-hoc derivation of effective k and c per Zhang's method (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021).

5. **Record tendon force time-histories** for all 9 tendons to identify energy partition and potential slack events, even in bare-cell runs.

6. **Include a gravity-loaded pre-drop equilibrium step** to capture tendon prestress state before impact.

7. **Test at least 3 orientations** (closed face, open face, double-rod) per the Zhang protocol, since orientation effects on effective stiffness range from 7–15.4 kN/m (pqac-00000021).

8. **For the egg-drop demo, include the egg mass as a minimum-fidelity lumped body** even at tier C—the mass ratio (egg/cell ≈ 80:1) is too extreme to omit.

9. **Validate MuJoCo contact parameters against a simple analytical case** (e.g., a single strut dropped on the floor) before running full prism simulations.

10. **Document all simulation floor parameters** (solref, solimp, timestep, friction) and their physical equivalents in every simulation log.

### 3(c) Rigid Floor Model Parameters

**Target physical properties** (ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 reinforced concrete pad with steel plate):
- **Concrete:** E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ = 2,300 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio ν ≈ 0.2 (pqac-00000045)
- **Steel impact plate:** E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (pqac-00000045)
- **Coefficient of friction:** μ_s ≈ 0.5–0.7 (PLA/TPU on steel), μ_d ≈ 0.4–0.5 (pqac-00000068) [*engineering judgment for polymer-on-steel*]
- **Coefficient of restitution:** e ≈ 0.5–0.6 for polymer-on-concrete (pqac-00000021)

**MuJoCo solref/solimp** (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000044):
- **solref:** Use `"0.002 1.0"` (current setting) or stiffer. The time constant of 0.002 s at damping ratio 1.0 produces very stiff, critically damped contacts. For truly rigid concrete, consider the negative format `solref="-1e6 -100"` (direct stiffness/damping specification) to enforce near-zero penetration [*engineering judgment*].
- **solimp:** Current `"0.98 0.999 0.0001"` sets high impedance (d0=0.98, dwidth=0.999, width=0.0001 m), which is appropriate for a rigid surface. The small width ensures rapid transition to full impedance. This is reasonable for concrete equivalence.
- **Friction:** Set `friction="0.6 0.005 0.0001"` (tangential, torsional, rolling) for PLA/TPU on steel/concrete.
- **Timestep:** With stiff contacts, use dt ≤ 0.001 s (preferably 0.0005 s) to avoid integration artifacts (pqac-00000047).

**PolyFEM+IPC barrier parameters** [*engineering judgment based on IPC methodology*]:
- **dhat (barrier thickness):** Set to 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻³ of the characteristic element length. For a 200 mm cell with ~2 mm element size, dhat ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻³ mm.
- **Floor material:** Model as linear elastic with E = 30 GPa (concrete) or 210 GPa (steel), ρ = 2,300 or 7,850 kg/m³ respectively.
- **Friction:** Coulomb μ = 0.5–0.6 with IPC's lagged friction update.
- **Floor mesh:** Fixed, thick slab (≥ 150 mm) with rigid base boundary conditions to approximate the effectively infinite mass required by ISO 2248.

### 3(d) Defensible PR Statement

> **"We leave the payload off in the current MuJoCo/tier-C simulations because the bare-cell screen is appropriate for topology and orientation ranking at this stage: the published tensegrity drop literature routinely validates protector architectures via bare-structure impact tests (Pajunen et al. 2019; Bauer et al. 2021; Vespignani et al. 2018), and our bare-cell results capture cell-dominated metrics (SEA, contact sequence, delocalization) that are the primary design levers at this fidelity level. However, for both the crutch-tip regime (75 kg, 1.4 m/s) and the NASA-lander regime (5 kg, 9.8 m/s), ASTM D5276 and GEVS respectively require the payload in the load path for any standards-facing claim, and our SDOF analysis shows the payload-to-cell mass ratio (≫1 for both regimes) places us firmly in the payload-dominated regime. We therefore plan to introduce explicit payload mass and mounting at tier B (DiffPD/Newton) and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC) before physical drop tests, and will conduct the physical drops with representative payload per ASTM D5276 / GEVS on a rigid floor (solref='0.002 1', solimp='0.98 0.999 0.0001', E_floor ≥ 25 GPa, friction μ = 0.5–0.6, matching the ISO 2248 unyielding surface specification). All bare-cell simulation results will co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload and include a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep at tier B to bound the rescaling error."**

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative observations about how payload mass and design choices affect impact response in tensegrity drop tests. Added mass (for example actuators or motors) increases impact forces yet does not help the impact response. Iterations toward a lighter, stiffer structure (carbon-fiber rods, tuned springs, TPU endcaps and shells) reduced peak payload accelerations and improved fatigue life, and some stationary prototypes survived drops up to 10 m. Improved endcaps and payload shells add energy absorption, but protection is chiefly from reduced mass and greater stiffness. Payloads can still contact rods or ground during impacts, causing payload damage (e.g., plastic payload fracturing) and limiting repeated-drop lifetime (some designs failed after ~5–10 drops). Protection depends on the payload’s vibrational mechanics—specifically its natural oscillating frequency—which is set by the payload-suspension stiffness and payload dynamics. Low oscillation frequency leads to larger deflections and collisions with the structure; high frequency leads to large accelerations on the payload. In their tests they varied suspension cable tension (coil count) and overall structure rigidity (pentagon side size) to tune stiffness and rigidity. They used eggs to proxy collision damage (most breaks from collisions), and note that in a ~10 m drop the structure landed at ~13.7 m/s while the egg saw an equivalent impact of ~2 m/s. Simulations/analysis showed a 6-bar tensegrity can keep payload peak decelerations below 25G even at a 15 m/s structure impact. The authors recommend symmetric, fully-connected suspension and accelerometers in future tests to better capture force-time histories.

Key findings: switching interior springs from k = 520 N/m to stiffer k = 740 N/m substantially increased rigidity and reduced payload collision severity; spring stiffening and lighter, stronger structural parts reduced catastrophic failures and doubled operational life to ~20 drops before spring replacement. contexts.context: The paper reports drop-test results for a 6-bar tensegrity (SUPERball v2-style) landing structure using an egg as proxy payload. Suspension-cable stiffness was parameterized by the number of coils (more coils = shorter/stiffer cable) and structural rigidity by pentagon side length (smaller pentagon = more rigid). Tests held one parameter constant while varying the other. With cable tension fixed at 3 coils, average failure (egg break) heights increased slightly as pentagon side increased: 22.33 ft (1.5 in), 23 ft (3 in), 24.67 ft (4.5 in). With pentagon side fixed at 3 in, increasing coils improved protection markedly: 2 coils → 5.33 ft average failure, 3 coils → 23 ft, 4 coils → 31.67 ft (~9.65 m). The structure landed at roughly 13.7 m/s for ~10 m drops, yet the egg experienced an equivalent impact of about 2 m/s (some casing padding). Prior data suggest eggs break at ~1.7 m/s (hard) and ~3.4 m/s (cushioned). Simulations cross-validated that payload decelerations can be kept <25G for ~15 m/s landings. Failures were often due to collisions with the structure; the report notes lack of accelerometer data and does not specify payload mass, recommending symmetric suspension and instrumentation for future tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes measurement methods and iterative design changes used in SUPERball prototypes relevant to drop tests. Spring deflection was measured using a mechanical-fuse thread method and a faster friction/paracord-crimp method (paracord secured above the payload to record irreversible cord extension). External linear springs produced experimental accelerations that roughly matched the computational model in magnitude, but exhibited extra oscillations not present in the model; high-speed video showed the springs oscillated axially and transversely due to spring mass and inertia. To address this, a third iteration moved linear springs inside the struts so they could oscillate only axially and the spring mass could be included in the strut mass. The chosen internal tension springs (music wire) required 10 lb to separate coils, had a spring constant of 23.5 lb/in, and were 1 in diameter and 9 in long; eyelets were set 59 in apart. A final internal-spring prototype could not be used for calibrated tests due to spring manufacturer error (springs had ~40 lb pre-tension vs expected ~10 lb) and lack of time to implement pulleys, causing high friction from eye-bolts. They kept total system mass fixed at 100 kg (70 kg payload, rods 5 kg each) and varied rod lengths to control the payload stroke and resulting deceleration. contexts.context: The SUPERball v2 student drop tests used an egg as a proxy payload; payload mass is not specified. Suspension cable 'stiffness' was varied by coiling fixed-length cables (metric = number of coils), and structure rigidity was varied via pentagon node side length (1.5 in, 3.0 in, 4.5 in). Two test matrices were run: constant tension (3 coils) while varying pentagon size, and constant pentagon size (3 in) while varying coil count (2, 3, 4). Results (failure heights where egg broke) show strong dependence on suspension pre-tension: for 3 in pentagons, average failure heights were ~5.33 ft (2 coils), ~23 ft (3 coils), and ~31.67 ft (4 coils, ~=9.65 m). For constant 3-coil tension, varying pentagon size produced average failure heights ~22.33 ft (1.5 in), ~23 ft (3 in), and ~24.67 ft (4.5 in). The authors report that in best tests the payload survived drops near 10 m; the whole structure impacted at about 13.7 m/s while the egg experienced an equivalent impact of ~2 m/s (egg break thresholds cited as ~1.7 m/s hard surface and ~3.4 m/s cushioned). Simulation/analysis indicated peak payload decelerations could be kept below ~25G for a 15 m/s landing.

contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes regulatory expectations for the impact surface in regulatory drop tests (UN/ADR/IMDG referencing ISO 2248): the surface must be horizontal, flat, immovable and unyielding. ISO 2248–referenced criteria include an impact target mass at least 50 times the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤2 mm, rigidity such that deformation does not exceed 0.1 mm under a 10 kg load applied over 100 mm², and sufficient area so the package lands fully on the surface. contexts.context: The excerpt frames the drop test as a globally standardized method to simulate impacts and assess whether dangerous-goods packaging can maintain containment under representative handling or accident events. It emphasizes that reliable outcomes depend not only on the package but also on the mechanical properties of the testing setup—particularly the impact surface or target—and that if the impact surface deforms or absorbs energy, test results may not reflect real-world conditions. The author identifies a shortfall in existing standards' guidance on impact-target specification and intent to revisit and refine the simplifying assumptions by explicitly examining the role of the impact target. The work proposes a revised evaluation framework that incorporates representative mechanical response characteristics of impact targets, citing parameters such as stiffness, energy absorption, and deformation behaviour under dynamic loading. The excerpt also cites UN Model Regulations findings that many cargo incidents stem from packaging failures, reinforcing the need for well-defined test setups.

contexts.context: The paper describes a drop-weight (free-fall striker) impact test on bare 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired lattice/tensegrity-like samples (no payload). Two striker masses (100 g and 200 g) were fabricated; experiments used the 200 g striker because it produced more consistent velocities. Impact velocity was controlled by drop height; an accelerometer on the striker and an oscilloscope recorded timing/forces, while a 1000 fps high-speed camera tracked displacement. Samples sat on a glass plate (acetone used to reduce friction); the force sensor measured reaction through the glass. Four samples (height 48.3 mm) were impacted multiple times at increasing velocities, so reusability/repeat-impact behavior was examined. Reported quasi-static/numerical metrics relevant to energy absorption: one redesigned geometry absorbed 3.1× the strain energy by 0.4 strain and normalized strain energy per mass increased ~3× (pin-jointed iteration), while the spherically-jointed design (mass 3.75 g vs pin-jointed 5.75 g) had ~1.5× higher normalized strain energy by mass. Structures densify at ~0.48 strain (struts touch). A dynamic ABAQUS beam model with the impact mass as point mass was also used to guide experiment velocities.

contexts.context: Zhang (2022) frames impact performance of tensegrity landers in terms of peak acceleration of a centrally suspended payload and highlights gaps in correlating board-level drop tests to product/system-level behavior and repeated-drop durability. For modeling impacts, Zhang contrasts impulse-momentum and Hertzian contact approaches and recommends a mass–spring–damper representation for flexible tensegrity systems because it captures elastic deformation and energy dissipation. The governing equation is m¨x + c ˙x + kx = −mg, and the model can derive effective stiffness (k) and damping (c) from two easily measured impact parameters: contact time (tc) and coefficient of restitution (e). The author cautions that stiffness and damping do not necessarily scale from quasi-static material tests, especially at high loading rates, motivating experimental calibration. Empirical drop tests on 22" tensegrity robots (1.5 m drops) were performed for three orientations (closed face, open face, double rod) with frame-by-frame video used to obtain tc and e. Reported mean values: tc = 0.040/0.033/0.027 s, e = 0.56/0.50/0.57, k = 7.0/10.4/15.4 kN/m and peak impact forces ≈ 360/508/524 N for the three orientations. Closed-face orientation gave the most flexibility and energy absorption.

contexts.context: The paper reports drop-weight testing of 3D-printed, tensegrity-inspired structures to evaluate dynamic impact response and reusability. Each sample was tested three times per impact energy, recording maximum force; the maximum force rises with impact energy but shows a distinct plateau, indicating load-limiting behavior. Energy dissipation during impact is substantial even at low energies and is quantified as Ed (dissipated energy as a percentage of impact energy). Dissipation sources include internal friction (hysteresis), plastic deformation, and test-setup damping, but experiments with two equivalent mass/velocity combinations produced absorbed momentum values within 1%, indicating the setup itself contributes little additional loss. The design aims for reusability: for the lower three impact energies strain after unloading is effectively zero, after each impact remaining strain is <0.2%, and after 24 impacts the average remaining strain is 2.28%, with most dissipated energy attributed to material hysteresis rather than plasticity. Energy-absorption metrics used are Wmin = Cmin * qr (qr = relative density, Cmin = cushion factor), with a target region of qr < 0.1 and Wmin < 0.21. The structure was not optimized for energy absorption but is compared to lattices, foams, and solids in Fig. 4.

contexts.context: Drop-weight tests were performed on 48.3 mm tall, 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired samples using a 200 g striker; impact energy Ei is reported as a fraction of the structure’s maximum strain energy before densification (Em = 320 mJ). Force–time curves (ABAQUS beam-element simulation vs experiments) show a short transmission lag, oscillations from stress waves and face rotations, and at higher Ei/Em a pronounced plateau corresponding to buckling — i.e., load-limiting behavior. Simulations (dashed) do not include hysteresis, so the plateau is more distinct in simulation than experiments, where hysteresis/internal friction reduces oscillations and causes different unloading. The structures are very low relative density (pin-jointed 4.9%, spherically-jointed 2.5%). Repeated-impact testing (four samples, multiple impacts) shows minimal plastic deformation and good reusability: total remaining strain after 24 impacts averages 2.28% (≈0.11% per impact), with about 3% residual strain at Ei/Em ≈ 0.81. Pin-jointed and spherically-jointed responses are similar, with some differences at high impact energies.

contexts.context: Pajunen et al. (2019) present a 3D-printable tensegrity-inspired structure that reproduces the compressive and impact behavior of prestressed buckling tensegrity systems. The work experimentally corroborates buckling-tensegrity responses and shows that the designed geometries give tensegrity-like characteristics without pin-joints or prestress. Impact testing indicates comparable quasi-static and dynamic responses to buckling tensegrity structures, with the spherically-jointed variant achieving the best energy absorption efficiency (Wmin) among the tested materials. The authors define energy absorption efficiency as the cushion factor multiplied by relative density, and report that their polymer structures lie within a target region (Wmin < 0.21, relative density < 0.1), exhibiting very low relative density and high energy-efficiency compared to solids and many lattices. Importantly, these designed structures elastically deform and are reusable under multiple impacts (unlike many lattices that plastically deform), and are producible with common single-material 3D-printing methods. The paper notes that raw/processed data to reproduce the findings are not publicly available at this time.

contexts.context: The excerpt explains two key shock-absorption metrics relevant to packaging drops: the Shock Response Spectrum (SRS) and cushion curves. SRS is defined as the maximum acceleration response of an array of single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillators (each with its own modal frequency) excited by a transient base input; Biot originally assumed the oscillators do not affect the base. Cushion curves plot deceleration of an impacting mass versus static stress and are used in the packaging industry to characterize foam impact performance; they vary with drop height and are traditionally generated experimentally. The paper notes an analytical approach: modeling shock response using a continuous rod approximation with a given impact velocity to generate cushion curves without exhaustive testing. contexts.context: The paper defines a delocalization efficiency ηd (ηd = 1: fully delocalized, ηd = 0: fully localized). Tensegrity metamaterials maintain highly delocalized deformation (ηd largely above 90%) and fully stable stress–strain responses across tested strains and relative densities, whereas the octet and Kelvin lattices show highly localized deformation and confined damage. The octet’s ηd drops (reported to as low as ~35% with increasing strain and down to ~29% in cyclic tests), and its elastic properties rapidly degrade under cyclic or increasing strain (a 10% increase in cycle strain caused ~55% stiffness and ~70% yield strength knockdown in the octet). By contrast, the tensegrity retained about 98% of initial stiffness and ~90% of yield strength under comparable cycling. At large strain the octet and Kelvin failed at ε = 2.6% and 17%, respectively, while the tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity until densification began at ε = 62.5%, corresponding to ~22× and ~4× greater deformability without failure versus octet and Kelvin. The authors report substantially higher damage resistance and much greater energy-absorption/deformability for tensegrity versus octet architectures.

contexts.context: The paper reports that space-tileable 3D tensegrity metamaterials (printed by TPP-DLW at 4–12% relative density) display markedly different deformation, failure, and energy-distribution behavior compared to octet truss and Kelvin foam architectures. The tensegrity maintains an even strain-energy distribution and shows no detectable localized damage up to 30% nominal compressive strain. Its stress–strain response is fully stable and monotonic, with a smooth, elongated post-yield plateau before densification above ≈62.5% strain. Quantitatively, the tensegrity sustained delocalization efficiencies above ηd = 90% across the test. By contrast, the octet exhibits localized, layer-by-layer deformation, with strains >2.6% producing localized fracture and plastic warping that concentrate strain energy, causing system-level instability and catastrophic stress drops; its ηd falls to ≈35% with increasing strain. The Kelvin foam also localizes (shear-type) above ≈17% strain. Overall, tensegrity topology delocalizes deformation, preventing localization-driven failure and providing a much more stable, distributed energy-absorption response than octet lattices at comparable conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that tensegrity metamaterials exhibit delocalized deformation that confers markedly superior damage resistance and energy absorption compared to octet (and Kelvin) continuous-compression lattices. Although the octet starts with much higher initial strength and stiffness (about 9× and 14× higher), its properties degrade rapidly with strain: at εc = 70% the octet retained only 7% of initial stiffness while the tensegrity retained 70%. The tensegrity retained load-bearing capacity up to densification at ε = 62.5%, representing a 22× and 4× increase in deformability without failure relative to octet and Kelvin. Experimentally the tensegrity absorbed ≈13× the energy of the octet; optimized and lower-density computational designs further amplify this advantage (absorbed energy before failure increased to 26× and, at very low relative density, up to 225× that of the octet). Simulations reproduce delocalized, stable stress–strain response for tensegrity versus localized, unstable failure in octet/Kelvin. The mechanism is that compressive-member instability in tensegrities can only propagate through tensile load paths, which do not buckle, suppressing localization and preventing progressive compressive failure that plagues continuous-compression lattices.

contexts.context: The excerpt introduces space-tileable tensegrity metamaterials designed to delocalize deformation by introducing a discontinuity in their compression members. This architectural feature prevents continuous compressive paths, which in turn inhibits localized failure propagation and produces a homogeneous, delocalized deformation distribution. The authors report dramatic improvements over comparable-strength state-of-the-art lattice architectures: up to a 25-fold enhancement in deformability and "orders of magnitude" increases in energy absorption capability without failure. The paper contrasts these tensegrity metamaterials with conventional stretching-dominated lattice designs, which typically exhibit unstable post-yield behavior (negative stiffness events) and catastrophic collapse once loaded beyond initial peak strength. Thus, the tensegrity design is presented as a pathway to failure-resistant, high-energy-absorbing lightweight structures by avoiding localized deformation and system-level instability.

contexts.context: Rosa et al. report that quasi-periodic (quasicrystalline) dual-lattice architectures develop delocalized force-chain distributions that both increase stiffness and enable stable post-buckling deformation, avoiding the unstable collapse often observed in periodic stretching-dominated lattices. Experimentally these dual lattices show relatively high stiffness, superior elastic energy absorption, and enhanced failure resistance under cyclic loading. The authors note that at ultra-low densities bending-dominated designs lose stiffness rapidly while periodic stretching-dominated designs remain largely unstable, implying quasi-periodic topologies can outperform typical periodic stretch-dominated lattices (e.g., octet) in stability and energy absorption, particularly at low relative density. Quasi-periodic designs also exhibit reduced sensitivity to imperfections due to lack of translational symmetry. Relevant metrics and methods useful for comparison include integrated energy absorption up to 50% strain or densification, a peak-instability metric (% peak drop), decomposition of beam energy into axial and bending components (with an axial polarization coefficient ϕ and per-beam energy indicator χ), and co-rotational beam FE simulations accounting for large displacements/rotations. Fabrication and material details (DLS UMA 90 resin, E≈484 MPa) and the cyclic-loading protocol are provided for experimental benchmarking.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports a bio-inspired curved-elliptical (BCE) lattice that achieves delocalized, bending-dominated deformation to avoid catastrophic collapse and improve energy absorption and deformation stability. BCE specimens were manufactured by SLM and tested in quasi-static compression with FE validation. At a relative density of 8% the BCE reaches a specific energy absorption (SEA) of 24.6 J/g, representing a 48.5% increase over the Octet lattice and a 297.6% increase over BCC. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a bio-inspired curved-elliptical (BCE) lattice that attains a stable, delocalized deformation mode by tuning the number (N) and amplitude (A) of strut waviness, thereby avoiding catastrophic collapse under compression. contexts.context: The excerpt explains MuJoCo contact/constraint tuning via solimp and solref. Constraints use stiffness k, damping b, and impedance d; these can be set per-constraint or left to defaults. Impedance d∈(0,1) (set via solimp) controls how strongly a constraint can generate force, is clamped to [mjMINIMP, mjMAXIMP] = [0.0001, 0.9999], and can vary with position using solimp = (d0, dwidth, width, midpoint, power) to provide softer behavior near contact onset and stiffer behavior under deeper penetration. For smooth, differentiable contact dynamics the text recommends d0 = 0 for limits and contacts. solref has two formats: positive (timeconst, dampratio) where timeconst acts as a softness control and the computed k and b are scaled by d(r) (so the specified timeconst/dampratio are exactly met only when d(r)=dwidth), and negative (−stiffness, −damping) which gives direct control over k and b and is useful for system identification or specific restitution behaviors. The excerpt does not provide a mapping from physical Young's modulus (e.g., concrete) to MuJoCo stiffness values.

snippets: In MuJoCo, the behavior of constraints is governed by three main parameters: stiffness k, damping b, and impedance d.
They can be defined individually for each constraint, applied through a defaults class, or left unset, in which case MuJoCo applies its internal default values.
The impedance d ∈(0, 1) quantifies the ability of the constraint to apply force.
It is defined through the solimp attribute, and internally clamped to [mjMINIMP, mjMAXIMP] = [0.0001, 0.9999].
solimp = (d0, dwidth, width, midpoint, power)
For smooth, differentiable contact dynamics, a setting of d0 = 0 is recommended for limits and contacts.
There are two formats for solref:
Positive format: (timeconst, dampratio)
Negative format: (−stiffness, −damping)
Because k and b are scaled by d(r), the specified time constant and damping ratio are exactly met only when d(r) = dwidth.
In the positive format, timeconst acts as a softness control, with larger values making the constraint less aggressive in resolving violations.
In the negative format, k and b can be tuned independently and are more suitable for system identification.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses identifying MuJoCo contact parameters (solref and solimp) on a cube-toss dataset. It shows that solref and solimp entries are per-index parameters (e.g., solref[0], solref[1], solimp[0] as d0, solimp[1] as dw, solimp[2] width, solimp[3] mid), indicating multiple tunable components. The authors observe that object geometry strongly affects impact timing (optimization moved the cube sidelength toward ~100 mm), and that contact-related parameter effects are interdependent: for instance, excessive mass causing larger penetrations during impacts can be mitigated by increasing constraint stiffness via solref[0] or solimp[0]. This implies solref/solimp control contact constraint stiffness/damping behavior and can be used to reduce penetration or make contacts appear stiffer in simulation. contexts.context: The excerpt explains MuJoCo's penalty-based contact formulation: contact forces are computed via a softened optimization that mixes minimizing unexpected accelerations and spring-damper corrections. Contacts are detected via a signed distance r(x) and are active when r(x) < 0. The solver uses two core functions: the impedance d(r) ∈ (0,1), a polynomial-spline function of constraint violation that “describes how strongly a constraint resists violation” and is parameterized by solimp = (do, dw, w, midpoint, power); and the position-level reference acceleration h(r), which defines how the solver corrects violations using velocity and position error and is controlled by solref parameters (time constant tc and damping ratio ϕd). Internally MuJoCo casts this as a convex optimization solved with a Newton method. The excerpt notes an in-depth description is available in Suppl. B.1. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a geometry-based approach that encodes element stiffness via a normalized shape factor É (0 = volume-preserving, 1 = rigid) (Eq. 5.4). This É provides a geometric proxy for mechanical stiffness: "introducing several materials with different shape factors É is similar to having elements with different stiffness E," enabling local tuning without modifying a global stiffness matrix. For hyperelastic (non-linear) materials, the framework requires two things: (1) obtaining the tangent or Young’s modulus at the current deformation, and (2) efficiently normalizing relative material properties to assign an appropriate É. The deformation gradient tensor F (and its principal stretches Σ) is used to compute an equivalent strain ϵeq per element; the tangent modulus is then found by taking the derivative of the stress–strain curve at that ϵeq. The text highlights the need to update É (or equivalent stiffness) per step to reflect non-linear behavior and notes the trade-off between accurate per-element stiffness updates and the computational cost of updating a global stiffness matrix. These points indicate a pathway to map physical Young’s modulus (or tangent modulus) into a normalized geometric stiffness parameter, and to compute per-element stiffness from hyperelastic models.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses regulatory expectations for drop-test impact surfaces similar to ASTM D5276’s requirement that the impact surface be rigid/flat/unyielding. It cites UN/ADR/IMDG references and ISO 2248 specifications: the impact target should have mass at least 50 times the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤2 mm, and rigidity such that a 100 mm² area loaded with 10 kg produces ≤0.1 mm static deformation. The text stresses that test outcomes depend on how kinetic energy is partitioned between package and impact surface, and notes that current regulations lack guidance on transient dynamic response (stress wave propagation, eigenfrequencies). It also cites an alternative criterion used for radioactive material packaging: a reinforced concrete foundation with solidly anchored steel plate of combined mass ≥10× specimen, and research showing transmitted energy into the target/ground <2%. The common practical design is a reinforced concrete foundation with an anchored steel impact plate. The excerpt raises questions about whether a fixed mass ratio (50×) is decisive and whether alternative design parameters could be used.

contexts.context: The provided excerpt does not cite ASTM D5276 or specify a concrete floor requirement. Instead, it describes a bespoke impact-target approach (Model Impact Targets, MITs) used to emulate a rigid foundation while limiting force transmission outward. The MIT design uses heavy steel plates (1 × 1 m with thicknesses 0.035, 0.070, 0.120 m) and large masses (280, 560, 960 kg) with spring elements whose stiffnesses were chosen to produce a maximum dynamic displacement of 2 mm and a purely elastic response for an 18 kg impact mass. The drop-test packages target a gross mass of 18 kg at ≥95% fill, using substitute fill materials (glass beads, PMMA granulate). Drop heights are governed by Packing Group per ADR: 1.8 m (PG I), 1.2 m (PG II), 0.8 m (PG III). Test positioning follows ISO 2206 impact-point definitions; e.g., the 1A2 steel drum is impacted at the tie rim (≈10° offset) and the 4G fibreboard box at a corner. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses vibration and shock test criteria and the role of drop tests. It recommends a 12-g shock of 0.080–0.100 s as a design criterion and notes a suggested sinusoidal vibration test of 5 g in three directions from 1 to 1000 cps. The authors state that proof tests (usually drop tests) are the final confirmation of design. With reference to MIL-STD-810 Table 516-1, a 24-inch drop is cited as producing about 100 g. However, the authors caution that drop tests are primarily applicable to assessing the integrity of shock-protected equipment when accidentally dropped, and may not represent the specific structural design requirements for shipping containers aboard aircraft—drop tests confirm gross survivability rather than define container design. They also note practical testing limits: a fully loaded container at 5 g requires a very large vibration table, so often only critical parts or assemblies are tested in a jig. contexts.context: The study performed free‑fall drop tests on filled polyethylene jerrycans. Tests used jerrycans filled with glycol (cooled to ~20–23°C and kept below the cited test‑standard requirement of 18°C) and measured temperature immediately after impact. The test rig released the harnessed jerrycan while a wagon ran on rails; slings were arranged so they did not constrain deformation or damp impacts. Because the wagon carried significant kinetic energy, aluminium honeycomb plates were installed to absorb the wagon impact energy so the wagon would not strike the jerrycan. A tray beneath the sample to catch leaks had its bottom cut out and sealed specifically so the impact would not be damped and the jerrycan could strike the foundation directly. The authors note small variations in impact velocity from rail friction, tilt and splices, and chose the large side wall as the critical impact orientation. Drop heights reached an equivalent free‑fall height up to 7.1 m without causing failure.

contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes key aspects of ASTM F1292 playground impact testing. The standard recognizes two equivalent test methods: ASTM F355 Procedure C (traditional) and the Free Fall Test Method. It measures two forces—Gmax and HIC—and considers three heights (Critical, Drop and Fall). Procedure C uses a head-shaped metal headform mounted to a rail or guide wires, instrumented with special electronic equipment; this instrumentation is described as cumbersome and expensive to deploy for field tests. A portable Free Fall Test instrument was developed and, per a six-laboratory round-robin, produced more repeatable/reproducible results than F355 Procedure C. Laboratory testing (including three-temperature tests) is used to determine the maximum drop height at which Gmax does not exceed 200 or HIC does not exceed 1000. Field tests at ambient temperature determine Gmax and HIC from the owner-specified drop height. The excerpt does not provide numeric headform mass or specific numeric drop heights for the Critical/Drop/Fall designations.

contexts.context: The excerpt summaries the historical basis and performance thresholds used in ASTM F1292 playground surfacing testing. contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes key elements of ASTM F1292 Laboratory and free-fall (Annex A1) testing. Laboratory acceptance criteria require that, using an average of the last two of three drops, no value exceed 200 g-max or 1000 HIC for tests at 30, 72 and 120°F. Impact tests are performed in one-foot increments up to a maximum drop height, with three drops at each increment; tests are also performed one foot above and below the maximum. contexts.context: The excerpt discusses an experimental study of impact targets used in packaging drop tests, explicitly addressing the "significance of the required 50 times mass ratio between impact target and test package." Two complementary methods are used: calculating the 50 % failure drop height (H50) for combinations of packaging type and impact target—using the Bruceton method (25 tests to estimate H50 and its standard deviation)—and numerical simulations combined with experimental drop testing to define deformability and kinetic energy transfer criteria. The study focuses on corrugated fibreboard boxes and steel drums, uses three model impact targets and two packaging design types, and defines packaging failure per ADR guidance. Experimental characterization methods listed include digital photogrammetry for flatness, experimental modal analysis (EMA) (here using a modal hammer and accelerometers due to practical constraints), DIC and accelerometers for kinematics, and impact force measurement. The text also describes deriving FRFs from FFTs of force and acceleration and using FRFs to assess impact-surface resistance, validate numerical models, and set thresholds for impact target foundations. Parameters of interest include restitution, eigenfrequency, damping, and dissipation.

contexts.context: The excerpt criticizes the ISO 2248 requirement that the impact target mass be at least 50 times the package (M/m ≥ 50), arguing this single mass-ratio rule does not assure a rigid, unyielding test surface and omits transient dynamic effects (kinetic energy transfer, energy restitution, ground strain). It recommends replacing the fixed mass-ratio requirement with technical criteria that consider the impact surface as an integrated foundation component whose geometry and mass must limit strain energy during the heaviest-package drop. Specific proposed provisions: (1) the impact surface must be part of a foundation behaving as a single mass with dimensions ensuring negligible strain energy; (2) if the impact surface component is <10% of total foundation thickness, only that component’s geometry is considered; (3) the required mass M should be determined via an energy-restitution-based factor α (so M ≥ α m) tied to a modified coefficient of restitution (e21), ground-strain limits, damping, and a safety factor. The approach allows estimating e21 from measured dmax or from initial shock response, making the mass-ratio requirement performance- and energy-based rather than a fixed number.

The primary issues with the current version of ISO 2248 can be summarized as follows:
Mass ratio as a singular criterion: The current specification of 𝑀/𝑚≥50 does not universally ensure the rigidity or stability of the impact target, particularly for heavy packages.

Foundation rigidity and integration: ISO 2248 lacks detailed guidelines on the foundation structure with a solidly anchored steel plate, leading to varied interpretations and potentially unreliable outcomes due to deviations in impact surface properties.
Neglect of transient dynamics: The standard does not address kinetic energy transfer, energy restitution, or the strain energy absorbed by the impact surface.
This work proposes an evaluation method based on kinetic energy transfer into the impact target structure resulting in ground strain energy.

Impact surface resistance and integration with foundation structure (NEW): The impact surface provided shall be part of a foundation structure (behaving as a single mass) with geometric dimensions that ensure negligible strain energy in a drop test with the heaviest package to be tested

Impact target composition (NEW): If the thickness of the foundation component comprising the impact surface is less than 10 % of the total thickness of the rest of the foundation components, then only  the geometric dimensions  of  the foundation component comprising the impact surface shall be considered under point 1.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Model Impact Targets (MITs) designed to be effectively rigid for package drop tests. Three steel-plate MITs (1 m × 1 m plates with thicknesses up to 0.120 m) have masses of 280, 560 and 960 kg. The test package gross mass is 18 kg, so the heaviest MIT produces a mass ratio of roughly 960/18 ≈ 53:1 (i.e., greater than 50:1). The MITs use spring elements with very high vertical stiffness (reported values ~14.7·10^6, 13.4·10^6, 12.1·10^6) and are sized so that maximum dynamic displacement is limited to 2 mm to ensure minimal deflection and a purely elastic response; relative static displacement is approximately zero. The design intent is to minimize force transmission outward and to simulate an installed foundation while treating mass ratio as an independent variable. The excerpt does not quote ISO 2248 or explicit regulatory language about using unyielding concrete/steel plates, but it documents an approach to achieve an effectively unyielding impact surface via large target mass, thick steel plate, and very stiff spring mounting.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes experimental model impact targets (MITs) used to study impact surface behavior in drop tests. MITs use three steel plates (280, 560, 980 kg) mounted on five low-damping spring elements and are tested against a fixed packaging gross mass of 18 kg, thereby exploring mass ratios up to roughly 54:1. Two complementary analysis approaches are used: (1) modal analysis and frequency response to establish rigidness criteria and thresholds for negligible elastic deformation so that energy restitution is dominated by the package, and (2) treating the impact pad plus subgrade as a rigid body oscillating vertically to evaluate maximum relative displacement and allowable kinetic energy. Numerical and experimental work aim to define a mass-ratio threshold between packaging and impact target, and to quantify kinetic energy dissipation through foundation and ground strain. Spring stiffness was chosen to limit dynamic displacement (noted target: 2 mm) to ensure minimal deflection. The excerpt does not explicitly cite ISO 2248 or state a prescriptive 50× mass ratio or a requirement for an unyielding concrete/steel plate, but it shows that the study intentionally includes a high (~50×) mass case and formulates criteria for what constitutes a sufficiently rigid impact surface.

contexts.context: Regulatory drop-test standards for dangerous goods (UN Model Regulations, ADR, RID, IMDG, IATA) require an essentially unyielding, horizontal, flat, immovable impact surface and reference ISO 2248 for detailed requirements. ISO 2248 (as cited) specifies: an impact target mass at least 50 times the heaviest package; flatness deviation not greater than 2 mm; rigidity such that static loading of 10 kg over 100 mm² causes no more than 0.1 mm deformation; and sufficient surface area for the package to land entirely on the plate. However, the regulations lack specifications for the dynamic mechanical response of the impact surface (transient impact loading, stress-wave propagation, eigenfrequencies), leaving potential ambiguity in design. For radioactive material (RAM) packaging, IAEA standards use a lower mass ratio (combined reinforced concrete foundation and steel plate at least 10 times the specimen) and studies have shown transmitted energy into the target/ground below ~2%, indicating practical unyielding behaviour. The excerpt notes practical problems for manufacturers who lack 50× foundations and highlights the need to consider alternative design parameters beyond a fixed mass ratio.

contexts.context: The excerpt summarizes ISO 2248 requirements and experimental validation for impact targets used in drop tests. ISO 2248 equivalence to a regulatory mass ratio is expressed as a maximum allowable energy transfer ratio δcrit = 1.96 %, which corresponds to an impact-target-to-package mass ratio M/m = 50 (worst-case complete energy transfer). The study used a steel plate (MIT–III) on the BAM foundation block as the impact plate and tested MITs with mass ratios of 15:1, 30:1 and 50:1; measured energy transfer percentages for these MITs were all well below the 1.96 % threshold, attributed to packaging deformation and dissipative filling. ISO 2248 also requires impact-surface flatness deviation not to exceed 2 mm; measured flatness values for MIT–I/II/III were 0.37, 0.25 and 0.22 mm respectively, meeting this criterion. Finally, ISO 2248 defines an "essentially unyielding" surface as deforming no more than xmax = 0.1 mm under a static 10 kg load applied over 100 mm2, a requirement used to assess local/global stiffness of impact surfaces.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are running tensegrity drop simulations (MuJoCo, Newton/Warp, PolyFEM+IPC)
and planning matching physical drop tests on a class-1 T-prism: 3 PLA struts
(rho ~ 1240 kg/m^3, E ~ 3.5 GPa) and 9 TPU 85A tendons (NinjaFlex-class:
E ~ 12 MPa secant, sigma_break ~ 26 MPa, rho ~ 1200 kg/m^3). Two regimes are
clamped to a Lansmont M23 envelope:

- `crutch_tip` (issue #18): 75 kg static payload through a Ø24 mm x 25 mm cell,
  impact velocity 1.4 m/s (~0.1 m drop), peak target <= 8 g (HAVS),
  pulse >= 5 ms.
- `nasa_lander` (issues #14, #16): 5 kg payload through a Ø200 mm x 200 mm cell,
  impact velocity 9.8 m/s (M23 max delta-V), peak target <= 1500 g (GSFC GEVS).

We have struggled with visualisation/simulation realism when the payload is
included. With the SUPERball / NASA-TBR architecture (payload sphere suspended
inside the cage by 6 additional TPU tendons), the soft 12 MPa TPU 85A
suspension oscillated wildly at impact and yanked the 0.7 g prism through the
rigid floor in MuJoCo. With the payload distributed across the struts as added
inertia (axial-load model, matching a crutch tip), the renders are stable and
look physical. The bare prism (no payload, just intrinsic strut/tendon mass)
is also stable. A reviewer therefore asked: **for these drop-tests, can we
just leave the payload off in the simulations**, and what does that cost us in
real-world applicability?

Please produce an in-depth, citation-rich brief that answers:

# 1. Physics of payload inclusion in drop simulations

  (a) Which impact-response metrics are dominated by the payload (mass,
      mounting, suspension stiffness) and which are dominated by the
      tensegrity cell itself? Cover at minimum: peak deceleration (g_max),
      pulse FWHM, specific energy absorption (SEA = E_abs / m_protector),

# Payload Inclusion in Tensegrity Drop Simulations: Physics, Standards, and Decision Rules

## 1. Physics of Payload Inclusion in Drop Simulations

### 1(a) Impact-Response Metrics: Payload vs Cell Dominance

The following table summarizes which metrics are governed primarily by the payload versus the tensegrity cell, the fidelity of no-payload simulations for each, and whether post-hoc rescaling is feasible.

It is useful for deciding what can be screened without payload and what must be simulated or tested with the payload in the load path.*

**Peak deceleration (g_max):** In the SUPERball architecture, simulations with a 100 kg system (70 kg payload, 5 kg per rod) at 15 m/s impact produced a peak payload deceleration of 21.4 G (agogino2018superballbotstructuresa pages 65-69, agogino2018superballbotstructures pages 65-69). Bayandor et al. showed that increasing payload from 180 kg to 260 kg at 10 m/s reduced peak g from 59.9 to 35.3 G—a direct consequence of the increased inertia lengthening the pulse and reducing peak acceleration at fixed kinetic energy (bayandor2017lightweightmultifunctionalplanetary pages 31-35). Zhang (2022) modeled this using m*ẍ + c*ẋ + k*x = −mg, deriving effective stiffness k and damping c from measured contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e; for the 22" tensegrity robot at 1.5 m drops, orientation-dependent effective stiffnesses ranged from 7.0 to 15.4 kN/m with contact times of 27–40 ms (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37, zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 33-37).

**Pulse FWHM:** Contact time is orientation-dependent but primarily cell-determined; payload mass lengthens the pulse through increased effective inertia. Zhang (2022) measured t_c = 27–40 ms across orientations for the 22" robot (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37).

**Specific energy absorption (SEA):** Primarily cell/topology-dominated when normalized per protector mass. Pajunen et al. (2019) showed that 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired structures at very low relative density (2.5–4.9%) achieve high energy-absorption efficiency (W_min < 0.21 at ρ_r < 0.1) using bare-structure drop-weight tests with a 200 g striker, with good reusability: average remaining strain of only 2.28% after 24 impacts (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 8-9). Bauer et al. (2021) demonstrated that tensegrity metamaterials absorb ~13× the energy of octet lattices experimentally, with delocalization efficiency η_d above 90% versus the octet's ~35% (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 3-6, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7).

**Volumetric efficiency (η_V):** Largely cell-dominated, governed by available stroke before densification (~62.5% strain for tensegrity metamaterials vs 2.6% for octet) (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 3-6, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7).

**Force-time history shape:** Mixed. The early contact plateau is cell-dominated, but payload mass/mounting creates secondary lobes, rebound pulses, and multi-hit signatures. Pajunen et al. observed that at higher impact energies, a pronounced plateau corresponding to buckling produces load-limiting behavior in simulation and experiment (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8).

**Contact-patch evolution:** Primarily cell-dominated through orientation and rod geometry. Zhang (2022) showed that closed-face, open-face, and double-rod orientations produce distinctly different contact mechanics (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37).

**Tendon strain energy distribution:** For main-cage tendons, cell-dominated; for internal suspension tendons, payload-dominated. Zhang (2022) noted that interior springs and the central payload "add a substantial amount of rigidity to the structure and play a critical role in impact protection" (zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 29-33, zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 29-33).

**Modal response:** The SUPERball egg-drop experiments demonstrated that suspension cable stiffness (parameterized by coil count) is the dominant factor in payload protection: increasing from 2 to 4 coils raised the average failure height from 5.33 ft to 31.67 ft (~9.65 m), while the structure impacted at ~13.7 m/s but the egg experienced only ~2 m/s equivalent (agogino2018superballbotstructuresa pages 73-77, agogino2018superballbotstructures pages 73-77). This highlights the critical importance of the payload drum mode frequency relative to the impact pulse frequency.
