### 1(c) Post-Hoc Rescaling

For a linear SDOF system, the classical cushion-packaging theory gives the peak acceleration as A_max = ω_n × V, where ω_n = √(k_eff/m_eff) and V is the impact velocity (zhong2013improvementofequivalent pages 6-9, zhong2013improvementofequivalent pages 1-4). Zhong et al. (2013) extended this with viscous and frictional damping coefficients: A_ff_max = u_ff × ω_n × V_0 + m_ff × ω_n × V_F, where u_ff and m_ff are correction factors derived from damping parameters (zhong2013improvementofequivalent pages 6-9). Zhang (2022) showed that effective k and c can be extracted from two measurable quantities—contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e—using the mass-spring-damper equation m*ẍ + c*ẋ + k*x = −mg (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37, zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 33-37).

The effective mass for rescaling follows m_eff = m_payload + α × m_cell, where α accounts for the fraction of cell mass participating in the impact DOF. For a class-1 T-prism with 3 struts, a reasonable first estimate is α ≈ 1/3 (one strut in the load path) for axial-tip loading (Mode A) [*engineering judgment*].

The Shock Response Spectrum (SRS) approach models the transient impact as exciting an array of SDOF oscillators at different natural frequencies, with the maximum response at each frequency defining the SRS envelope (joodaky2020mechanicsanddesign pages 15-19). This is applicable for converting bare-cell impact pulses to payload response predictions when the mounting can be approximated as linear.

**Rescaling is reliable** when: (i) the system is well-approximated by a single-DOF (contact time t_c ≫ payload natural period T_p, or T_p ≫ t_c); (ii) no tendon slack, internal collision, or mode switching occurs; (iii) the mass ratio m_payload/m_cell < ~3. **Rescaling breaks down** when: (i) payload and cell natural frequencies are comparable (0.3 < ω_p/ω_impact < 3); (ii) soft TPU tendons allow large relative displacement; (iii) the payload can collide with the cage structure.

### 1(d) TPU 85A Tendon Stiffness/Mass Thresholds

Printed NinjaFlex 85A (TPU Shore 85A) has a measured tensile modulus of ~11 MPa (georgopoulou2021fabricationofa pages 5-6), consistent with the user-stated E ≈ 12 MPa. For a single TPU tendon of cross-section A and free length L, the axial stiffness is k_cable = E × A / L. For the user's T-prism with 9 tendons, assuming a typical tendon diameter of ~2 mm (A ≈ 3.14 mm²) and free length ~150 mm [*engineering estimate for Ø200 mm cell*]:

k_cable ≈ 12 × 10⁶ × 3.14 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.15 ≈ 251 N/m per tendon

With ~3 tendons effectively in the load path for a given orientation, k_eff ≈ 750 N/m. The natural frequency of the payload on this suspension is:

- **Crutch tip (75 kg):** ω_n = √(750/75) ≈ 3.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 0.5 Hz → T_n ≈ 2 s. This is vastly longer than any impact pulse (~5–40 ms), meaning the cell response completes before the payload responds: the system is **cell-dominated** for the contact event itself, but the payload mass overwhelms the 0.7 g prism mass by a factor of ~100,000:1, making the axial loading physics entirely payload-driven.

- **NASA lander (5 kg):** ω_n = √(750/5) ≈ 12.2 rad/s → f_n ≈ 1.9 Hz → T_n ≈ 0.5 s. Still much longer than the ~5–30 ms contact pulse.

For internal suspension (Mode C) with stiffer, shorter cables (e.g., k_susp ≈ 5–10 kN/m as in SUPERball), the payload drum-mode frequency rises into the 5–50 Hz range, approaching the impact pulse bandwidth. The critical transition occurs when ω_p/ω_impact ≈ 1, i.e., √(k_susp/m_payload) ≈ π/t_c. For t_c ≈ 30 ms, ω_impact ≈ 105 rad/s; equating gives k_susp/m_payload ≈ 11,000 s⁻², or m_payload_crit ≈ k_susp/11,000. With k_susp = 750 N/m (soft TPU), m_payload_crit ≈ 0.07 kg—meaning **any payload above ~70 g on soft TPU 85A tendons will be in the payload-dominated regime** for typical tensegrity impact pulses [*engineering judgment from SDOF analysis*]. This explains the MuJoCo instability observed with the 0.7 g prism: the soft 12 MPa TPU suspension combined with the payload creates a very low-frequency internal mode that oscillates wildly relative to the fast contact event, yanking the prism through the floor.

## 2. Real-World Applicability and Standards Mapping

### 2(a) Standards Requirements

**ASTM D5276 (Free-Fall Drop of Loaded Containers):** Explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** (i.e., payload present) during the drop. The impact surface must be rigid, flat, unyielding, and immovable (schulerUnknownyearrecentbritishdevelopments pages 171-176, menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7, grabowskiUnknownyeardesignandevaluation pages 171-176). Per ISO 2248 (referenced by D5276 and UN/ADR/IMDG), the impact target mass must be at least 50× the heaviest package, flatness deviation ≤ 2 mm, and static deformation ≤ 0.1 mm under 10 kg applied over 100 mm² (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32, lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82). Practical implementation uses a reinforced concrete foundation with anchored steel impact plate; the BAM test facility uses an 18,000 kg steel-reinforced concrete block (menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7). Lengas (2025) showed the 50× ratio corresponds to a maximum energy transfer of 1.96% (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82).

**ASTM F1292 (Playground Impact Attenuation):** Uses an instrumented headform (surrogate payload) dropped onto the surface under test. Acceptance criteria: G_max ≤ 200 g and HIC ≤ 1000 (huber2001playgroundsurfacing pages 17-19, huber2001playgroundsurfacing pages 19-21, huber2011impactattenuationvalues pages 7-9, olsen2018finalreportfor pages 30-33). Three drops per site; average of drops 2 and 3 is used. Laboratory tests at three temperatures (30, 72, 120°F) with preconditioning (huber2001playgroundsurfacing pages 19-21). This standard tests the **surface**, not the falling object—the headform IS the payload.

**ASTM F2971 (AM Test Reporting):** Addresses reporting of additive manufacturing test specimens; does not prescribe drop-test conditions but requires reporting of build orientation, process parameters, and material properties.

**ISTA 1A/1H:** Non-simulation transit tests for packaged products. ISTA 1A requires loaded containers dropped on a rigid surface from heights keyed to package mass. Payload must be present.

**MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8 (Shock):** Defines transit drop, crash hazard, and handling shock procedures. The standard requires the test item to be in its deployment/shipping configuration, meaning payload or mass surrogate matched to mass and CG must be present. A 24-inch drop produces approximately 100 g (wood1965designcriteriatechnical pages 102-106).

**GSFC GEVS-STD-7000B:** Specifies vibration, shock, and acoustic test levels for spacecraft and payloads. Shock tests are performed at the component, instrument, and spacecraft level with the actual hardware or mass/CG-matched surrogates. Qualification levels are typically +3 dB above acceptance levels on the SRS envelope.

**ISO 2248:** Defines the unyielding surface specification: mass ratio ≥ 50× package, flatness ≤ 2 mm, deformation ≤ 0.1 mm (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32, lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82). For radioactive material packaging (IAEA), the requirement is relaxed to ≥ 10× specimen with combined reinforced concrete and steel plate (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32).

### 2(b) Conventions in Published Tensegrity Drop Literature

**Zhang 2022 (22-inch, 20 m, 20-drop life):** Used a centrally suspended sensor payload as the primary test article; peak payload acceleration was the acceptance metric. Interior spring stiffness (k = 520→740 N/m) was the key tuning parameter. Drops were conducted **with payload** (zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 29-33, zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 29-33, zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 52-58, zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 52-58, zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37, zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 25-29, zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 25-29).

**Agogino 2018 / SunSpiral 2015 (SUPERball NIAC Phase 2):** Simulations used a 70 kg payload in a 100 kg system. Physical egg-drop tests used an egg as proxy payload suspended by cables, **without accelerometers**—failure was binary (egg broke or not). Payload mass was not explicitly reported for physical tests (agogino2018superballbotstructuresa pages 73-77, agogino2018superballbotstructuresa pages 65-69, agogino2018superballbotstructures pages 65-69, sunspiral2015superballbotstructures pages 72-75, agogino2018superballbotstructures pages 73-77).

**Vespignani 2018 (SUPERball v2):** Physical drop tests at up to 8 m/s were conducted **without payload**; the paper states "Future experiments will also include a test payload system" (vespignani2018designofsuperball pages 1-2).

**Pajunen 2019 (3D-printed tensegrity-inspired, 24-impact reuse):** All tests were bare-structure drop-weight impacts using a 200 g striker—**no internal payload**. The work characterized SEA, reusability, and load-limiting behavior of the protector material itself (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 5-7, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 8-9, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 1-2).

**Bauer 2021 (tensegrity vs octet metamaterials):** Quasi-static compression testing only, **bare metamaterial lattice** with no payload. Demonstrated 25× deformability enhancement and 13× energy absorption advantage for tensegrity over octet (bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 3-6, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 2-3, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 6-7, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 8-9, bauer2021tensegritymetamaterialstoward pages 1-2).

**Bayandor 2017 (BEAR/NIAC probe):** Parametric simulation with explicit payload masses (180 kg and 260 kg) at 10–30 m/s. **Payload was always included** in simulations (bayandor2017lightweightmultifunctionalplanetary pages 31-35).

**Summary:** The community convention is mixed. Simulation-focused studies (Agogino, Bayandor, Zhang) typically include the payload. Experimental studies of the protector material itself (Pajunen, Bauer) and early hardware validation (Vespignani) often use bare structures. No published tensegrity drop paper we identified reports both payload-laden and bare-cell experimental results side-by-side.

### 2(c) Standards Requirements for Your Two Regimes

**Crutch tip / ASTM D5276:** The standard explicitly requires the container to be **loaded** during the drop, onto a rigid, flat, unyielding surface (schulerUnknownyearrecentbritishdevelopments pages 171-176, menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7). For your 75 kg payload, the impact surface must have mass ≥ 50 × 75 = 3,750 kg per ISO 2248 (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 30-32, lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 78-82). Your current MuJoCo rigid floor is mathematically equivalent to infinite mass and zero deformation—this is **more conservative** than the standard's concrete pad. However, a physical test requires a concrete or steel foundation meeting the ≥ 50× mass ratio and ≤ 0.1 mm deformation criteria.

**NASA lander / GEVS:** GEVS requires the flight article or a mass/CG-matched surrogate to be present during shock qualification. For a 5 kg payload at 9.8 m/s, the payload must be in the load path. The impact surface in GEVS is typically a rigid fixture or pyrotechnic shock table; for drop-test equivalence, the same ISO 2248 unyielding criteria apply.

**Floor surface specification:** The standard concrete pad has E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ ≈ 2,300 kg/m³ (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 154-161), typically ≥ 150 mm thick on a foundation block ≥ 1 m³. The BAM facility uses an 18,000 kg reinforced concrete block with anchored steel plate (menrad2014droptestof pages 7-7). Steel plate has E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 154-161).

### 2(d) Egg-Drop Demo Path

The egg-drop protocol (Ø 200 mm bounding sphere, m_sys ≤ 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per ASTM D5276) places the egg mass at ~11% of system mass—well above the 70 g threshold for payload-dominated response on soft TPU tendons (Section 1d). **A payload-free simulation cannot be defended as predictive of the egg-laden drop** because: (i) the egg introduces a ~55 g concentrated mass that dominates the T-prism's ~0.7 g intrinsic mass; (ii) the egg's mounting (cradle/suspension) creates the critical internal mode; (iii) the acceptance criterion is egg survival, which depends entirely on payload-experienced g. The SUPERball egg-drop experiments confirm this: suspension stiffness was the dominant factor in egg survival, not cage topology alone (agogino2018superballbotstructuresa pages 73-77, agogino2018superballbotstructures pages 73-77).

**Protocol amendment for bare-cell screening tier:** If bare-cell simulations are used as the screening tier, the protocol should: (1) explicitly state that bare-cell runs screen topology and orientation only; (2) require reporting of m_eff = m_cell + m_egg + m_cradle; (3) require a minimum 2-point payload sensitivity sweep (0× and 1× egg mass) at tier B before physical testing; (4) require the physical drop to include the egg per D5276; (5) define pass/fail at the physical drop, not the bare-cell sim.

## 3. Recommendations and Decision Rules

### 3(a) Simulation Tier Decision Rules

**Tier C (MuJoCo/NTRT rigid screening):** Use bare-cell (Mode D) simulations for topology ranking, orientation sensitivity, and contact-sequence screening. Acceptable for all four mounting modes only if results are labeled "topology screen—not predictive of payload g." For Mode A (crutch), distributed inertia matching total mass is acceptable. For Mode C (suspended), bare cage only.

**Tier B (DiffPD/Newton mid-fidelity):** Include explicit payload mass and mounting stiffness for all modes. Mode A: lumped mass at tip or distributed inertia. Mode B: rigid body on strut. Mode C: suspended mass with calibrated k_susp and collision constraints. Mode D: promote to explicit payload sweep.

**Tier A (PolyFEM+IPC high-fidelity):** Full payload geometry, material nonlinearity, contact with friction, and standard-compliant floor model. Required for any publication-grade or standards-facing claim about payload survivability.

### 3(b) Design Changes to Maximize Predictive Value of Bare-Cell Simulations

1. **Always co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload** alongside bare-cell metrics so that results can be rescaled via the SDOF model A_max ≈ ω_n × V = √(k_eff/m_eff) × V (zhong2013improvementofequivalent pages 6-9, zhong2013improvementofequivalent pages 1-4).

2. **Run a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep** (0× and 1× design payload) at tier B for every finalist topology before physical testing.

3. **Simulate on a rigid floor matching ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 specification** (see 3c below) rather than a default MuJoCo floor.

4. **Report contact time t_c and coefficient of restitution e** from every simulation; these allow post-hoc derivation of effective k and c per Zhang's method (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37, zhang2022designofimpactresistant pages 33-37).

5. **Record tendon force time-histories** for all 9 tendons to identify energy partition and potential slack events, even in bare-cell runs.

6. **Include a gravity-loaded pre-drop equilibrium step** to capture tendon prestress state before impact.

7. **Test at least 3 orientations** (closed face, open face, double-rod) per the Zhang protocol, since orientation effects on effective stiffness range from 7–15.4 kN/m (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37).

8. **For the egg-drop demo, include the egg mass as a minimum-fidelity lumped body** even at tier C—the mass ratio (egg/cell ≈ 80:1) is too extreme to omit.

9. **Validate MuJoCo contact parameters against a simple analytical case** (e.g., a single strut dropped on the floor) before running full prism simulations.

10. **Document all simulation floor parameters** (solref, solimp, timestep, friction) and their physical equivalents in every simulation log.

### 3(c) Rigid Floor Model Parameters

**Target physical properties** (ASTM D5276/ISO 2248 reinforced concrete pad with steel plate):
- **Concrete:** E ≈ 25–30 GPa, ρ = 2,300 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio ν ≈ 0.2 (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 154-161)
- **Steel impact plate:** E = 210 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³ (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 154-161)
- **Coefficient of friction:** μ_s ≈ 0.5–0.7 (PLA/TPU on steel), μ_d ≈ 0.4–0.5 (lengas2025parameterstudyof pages 107-111) [*engineering judgment for polymer-on-steel*]
- **Coefficient of restitution:** e ≈ 0.5–0.6 for polymer-on-concrete (zhang2022designofimpactresistanta pages 33-37)

**MuJoCo solref/solimp** (yaman2025designmodelingand pages 119-122, yaman2025designmodelingand pages 113-119, paulus2025differentiablesimulationof pages 3-4):
- **solref:** Use `"0.002 1.0"` (current setting) or stiffer. The time constant of 0.002 s at damping ratio 1.0 produces very stiff, critically damped contacts. For truly rigid concrete, consider the negative format `solref="-1e6 -100"` (direct stiffness/damping specification) to enforce near-zero penetration [*engineering judgment*].
- **solimp:** Current `"0.98 0.999 0.0001"` sets high impedance (d0=0.98, dwidth=0.999, width=0.0001 m), which is appropriate for a rigid surface. The small width ensures rapid transition to full impedance. This is reasonable for concrete equivalence.
- **Friction:** Set `friction="0.6 0.005 0.0001"` (tangential, torsional, rolling) for PLA/TPU on steel/concrete.
- **Timestep:** With stiff contacts, use dt ≤ 0.001 s (preferably 0.0005 s) to avoid integration artifacts (paulus2025differentiablesimulationof pages 13-15).

**PolyFEM+IPC barrier parameters** [*engineering judgment based on IPC methodology*]:
- **dhat (barrier thickness):** Set to 1×10⁻⁴ to 1×10⁻³ of the characteristic element length. For a 200 mm cell with ~2 mm element size, dhat ≈ 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻³ mm.
- **Floor material:** Model as linear elastic with E = 30 GPa (concrete) or 210 GPa (steel), ρ = 2,300 or 7,850 kg/m³ respectively.
- **Friction:** Coulomb μ = 0.5–0.6 with IPC's lagged friction update.
- **Floor mesh:** Fixed, thick slab (≥ 150 mm) with rigid base boundary conditions to approximate the effectively infinite mass required by ISO 2248.

### 3(d) Defensible PR Statement

> **"We leave the payload off in the current MuJoCo/tier-C simulations because the bare-cell screen is appropriate for topology and orientation ranking at this stage: the published tensegrity drop literature routinely validates protector architectures via bare-structure impact tests (Pajunen et al. 2019; Bauer et al. 2021; Vespignani et al. 2018), and our bare-cell results capture cell-dominated metrics (SEA, contact sequence, delocalization) that are the primary design levers at this fidelity level. However, for both the crutch-tip regime (75 kg, 1.4 m/s) and the NASA-lander regime (5 kg, 9.8 m/s), ASTM D5276 and GEVS respectively require the payload in the load path for any standards-facing claim, and our SDOF analysis shows the payload-to-cell mass ratio (≫1 for both regimes) places us firmly in the payload-dominated regime. We therefore plan to introduce explicit payload mass and mounting at tier B (DiffPD/Newton) and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC) before physical drop tests, and will conduct the physical drops with representative payload per ASTM D5276 / GEVS on a rigid floor (solref='0.002 1', solimp='0.98 0.999 0.0001', E_floor ≥ 25 GPa, friction μ = 0.5–0.6, matching the ISO 2248 unyielding surface specification). All bare-cell simulation results will co-report m_eff = m_cell + m_payload and include a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep at tier B to bound the rescaling error."**

| Metric | Dominated By (Payload vs Cell) | No-Payload Simulation Fidelity | Rescaling Feasibility | Key References |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peak deceleration ($g_{max}$) | Usually payload mass + mounting stiffness once the payload is in the load path; cell topology/orientation still matters because it sets stopping distance and effective stiffness. Suspended payloads are especially payload-dominated; distributed/axial loading is more mixed. | **Moderate** for axial-load or distributed-inertia cases; **poor** for internally suspended payloads, where omission can underpredict internal relative motion or miss secondary impacts. | **Good** if response is close to SDOF and mounting stiffness is known: $g_{max}\sim \omega_n V$ or can be re-fit with effective $m$-$k$-$c$ from contact time and restitution; weak if strong mode switching or slack/tendon collision occurs. | (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000031) |
| Pulse FWHM | Mixed, but more cell-dominated than $g_{max}$ because it tracks global compliance/stroke; payload mass lengthens the pulse when it increases effective inertia, while stiff mounting shortens it. | **Moderate to good** for rigidly attached or axially applied payloads if geometry/orientation are preserved; **poor to moderate** for soft suspended payloads because internal oscillation can split or broaden the pulse. | **Moderate** via equivalent $m$-$k$-$c$ calibration from measured contact time $t_c$ and restitution; weaker when multiple pulses arise from rebound or internal collisions. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028) |
| Specific energy absorption (SEA) | Primarily cell/material/topology-dominated when defined per protector mass; payload changes the operating point and total absorbed energy but not the intrinsic absorber mass basis. | **Good** for ranking architectures/topologies and protector concepts; **moderate** for predicting absolute absorbed energy in a payload-qualified test. | **Moderate** by scaling input energy $mgh$ or $\tfrac12 mV^2$ at fixed protector mass; not sufficient if payload changes deformation pathway or densification onset. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000039) |
| Volumetric efficiency ($\eta_V$) | Mostly cell-dominated because it is governed by geometry, available stroke, and deformation delocalization; payload mainly selects where on the response curve the cell operates. | **High** for topology screening and geometric comparisons, provided bounding volume and impact orientation are matched. | **Limited to moderate**; can scale with absorbed energy at common volume, but payload-induced localization or bottoming can shift the ranking near densification. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039) |
| Force-time history shape | Strongly mixed: early contact and plateau behavior are cell-dominated, but payload mass/mounting strongly affect peak count, secondary lobes, rebound, and shock-pulse shape. Suspended payloads can create multimodal or double-hit signatures. | **Moderate** for bare-cell contact mechanics and load-limiting plateaus; **poor** for predicting full waveform under suspended or off-CG payloads. | **Moderate** with SRS/SDOF or equivalent-drop methods for single-mode pulses; **poor** for multi-lobed histories with slack tendons, internal impacts, or secondary contact. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030) |
| Contact-patch evolution | Primarily cell-dominated through orientation, rod/endcap geometry, and global compliance; payload affects patch indirectly by changing attitude evolution and local load concentration. | **Good** for bare-cell orientation studies and topology screening if mass distribution is not drastically altered; **moderate to poor** when payload shifts CG enough to change landing attitude or induce floor pull-through artifacts. | **Poor to limited**; post-hoc scaling cannot reliably recover altered contact sequence once the payload changes attitude dynamics or local indentation sequence. | (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021) |
| Tendon strain energy distribution | Strongly cell- and topology-dominated for the main cage, but very payload-dominated for any dedicated suspension tendons. Soft suspended payloads can siphon energy into a drum mode and create large asymmetries. | **Good** for main-cage tendon ranking in bare-cell screens; **poor** for internal-suspension designs because the omitted payload removes the very tendons and energy path of interest. | **Limited** for main cage via effective stiffness updates; **poor** for suspended payload architectures because energy partition among cage vs suspension tendons is topology-specific and nonlinear. | (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) |
| Modal response (drum mode of suspended payload vs cell breathing mode) | Dominated by the relative stiffness/mass ratio between payload suspension and cell. Cell breathing modes are cell-dominated; suspended-payload drum modes are payload-dominated and can overwhelm global impact response when frequencies are comparable. | **High** for breathing-mode identification of the bare cell; **very poor** as a surrogate for suspended-payload dynamics because omitting the payload deletes the critical internal mode. | **Moderate** only if modal separation is clear and a two-DOF model is adequate; **poor** when frequencies are close, tendons go slack, or internal collisions occur. | (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) |


*Table: This table summarizes which drop-response metrics are governed mainly by the payload versus the tensegrity cell, how trustworthy bare-cell simulations are for each metric, and when post-hoc rescaling is plausible. It is useful for deciding what can be screened without payload and what must be simulated or tested with the payload in the load path.*

| Mounting Mode | Description | Faithful Regime (no-payload OK) | Misleading Regime (payload required) | Explicit Threshold | Simulation Tier Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Axially-loaded strut tip (crutch use case) | External load enters through one tip or cell into the main compressive path; physically closest to a tip-loaded protector or crutch ferrule, and often well-approximated by distributed added inertia along struts if the payload hardware is much stiffer than the cell. | Bare-cell or distributed-inertia sim is usually acceptable when the payload acts quasi-statically on the axial path, CG remains near the strut axis, local mounting compliance is negligible, and the added mass does not create a new internal mode. Best use: comparing orientations, tendon prestrain, and gross pulse-shaping trends. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000021) | Misleading when the tip hardware itself is compliant, offset, or massive enough to rotate the cell; when local crushing or contact area at the tip matters; when the load path bypasses the nominal tensegrity mode and produces local bending; or when acceptance is on occupant or payload g rather than cell g. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) | Rule of thumb: no-payload surrogate is defensible if m_payload/m_cell <= 1 or if the payload is represented as distributed axial inertia with matched total mass and CG. It becomes risky for absolute g_max once m_payload/m_cell >= 3, and generally unacceptable beyond about 10 without explicit mass inclusion. Engineering judgment, anchored by SDOF scaling where omega_n = sqrt(k_eff/m_eff). (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000031) | Tier C: OK to omit payload only for topology or orientation screening if total effective mass is reported separately. Tier B: include lumped mass or distributed inertia matched to mass and CG. Tier A: include real load applicator and contact patch for any claim about crutch-tip pulse, HAVS peak g, or pulse width. |
| B. Payload rigidly clamped to one strut (instrumented accelerometer mass) | A concentrated lumped mass is attached to one strut, common in tensegrity robot logs; changes local bending, strut inertia, and CG more than a purely axial load. | Bare-cell sim can still rank topologies if the attached mass is small enough that it does not appreciably perturb mode shapes or contact sequence; acceptable for qualitative stability and first-pass contact or orientation screening. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021) | Misleading when the clamp mass is not negligible relative to the cell, when it shifts CG off-center, when local strut bending or torsion matters, or when the instrument mass is used to infer payload survivability. Even modest asymmetry can raise peak accelerations and alter orientation sensitivity. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) | Rule of thumb: faithful if attached mass on one strut is less than 5 percent of system mass and m_payload/m_cell <= 0.1; caution for 0.1 to 0.3; payload must be modeled for m_payload/m_cell >= 0.3 or if CG offset exceeds about 5 percent of cell radius. Engineering judgment extrapolated from asymmetric-mass sensitivity in tensegrity lander tests. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013) | Tier C: omit only if the attached sensor mass is truly tiny; otherwise add a lumped body to the strut. Tier B: model the rigid clamp and local bending inertia. Tier A: always include explicit clamp or body or contact coupling if reporting strut acceleration, local stress, or failure risk. |
| C. Payload suspended inside cage by TPU tendons (SUPERball or NASA-TBR style) | Internal payload hangs on a secondary, very soft tendon network; introduces a second DOF family, payload drum mode, coupled to cell breathing and contact modes. This is the architecture most sensitive to payload omission. | No-payload simulation is only faithful for narrow questions about the outer cage alone: for example, bare-cell self-contact stability, cage-first-contact orientation ranking, or manufacturability or topology screens where internal payload protection is explicitly out of scope. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) | Misleading for nearly all payload-relevant metrics: payload g_max, pulse splitting, secondary impacts, tendon energy partition, and internal collisions. SUPERball studies show suspension stiffness strongly changes survivable height; too-soft suspension lets the payload deflect into the cage, too-stiff suspension raises payload acceleration. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000011) | Strong threshold from modal separation: let omega_p = sqrt(k_susp/m_payload) and impact frequency omega_imp approximately pi/t_c. Bare-cell surrogate is only plausible if omega_p/omega_imp > 3 or < 0.3 and the payload cannot strike the cage; if 0.3 <= omega_p/omega_imp <= 3, response is payload-dominated and the payload must be modeled. Mass-ratio threshold is severe for soft TPU: with NinjaFlex-class E about 11 to 12 MPa, even modest payloads dominate once m_payload/m_cell >= 0.3, and certainly for >= 1. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000048) | Tier C: do not use for predictive payload claims; at most use for cage-only screening. Tier B: minimum acceptable tier for suspended-payload response and must include payload mass, suspension stiffness, damping, and collision limits. Tier A: required for any publication-grade prediction of lander payload g, tendon load share, or internal collision risk. |
| D. Bare cell plus fictitious added inertia (topology screen) | A deliberately simplified screen where the payload is omitted but total mass or effective inertia is approximated by fictitious added mass or distributed inertia; intended for fast architecture ranking rather than direct test prediction. | Appropriate when the objective is relative comparison among geometries, prestress levels, or materials under the same effective mass budget; also useful when ranking SEA, delocalization, and volumetric efficiency of the protector itself rather than payload survivability. Pajunen and Bauer-style bare-structure tests fit this regime. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034) | Misleading if presented as direct evidence for a specific payloaded drop without calibration; especially poor where mounting topology matters, CG matters, or a real payload creates new modes or contact events. Bare-cell performance can rank a topology correctly yet still miss absolute payload g by a large margin. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000012) | Defensible if framed as a screening tier and paired with post-hoc rescaling using m_eff = m_cell + alpha m_payload and or calibrated m-k-c fits; best when alpha and CG are reported and a 2-point payload sensitivity sweep is run. Safest for relative ranking up to about m_payload/m_cell ~ 1; beyond that, absolute predictions need explicit payload models. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000031) | Tier C: recommended default for rapid topology screening only; explicitly label as non-predictive for payload survivability. Tier B: promote finalists to explicit payload sweeps. Tier A: never stop at fictitious inertia if the goal is standards-facing or real-world acceptance claims. |


*Table: This matrix summarizes when no-payload simulations are acceptable surrogates and when they become misleading for four common tensegrity payload-mounting modes. It is useful for deciding what can remain in the fast screening tier versus what must be promoted to payload-inclusive mid- and high-fidelity simulation.*

info.query:
We are running tensegrity drop simulations (MuJoCo, Newton/Warp, PolyFEM+IPC)
and planning matching physical drop tests on a class-1 T-prism: 3 PLA struts
(rho ~ 1240 kg/m^3, E ~ 3.5 GPa) and 9 TPU 85A tendons (NinjaFlex-class:
E ~ 12 MPa secant, sigma_break ~ 26 MPa, rho ~ 1200 kg/m^3). Two regimes are
clamped to a Lansmont M23 envelope:

- `crutch_tip` (issue #18): 75 kg static payload through a Ø24 mm x 25 mm cell,
  impact velocity 1.4 m/s (~0.1 m drop), peak target <= 8 g (HAVS),
  pulse >= 5 ms.
- `nasa_lander` (issues #14, #16): 5 kg payload through a Ø200 mm x 200 mm cell,
  impact velocity 9.8 m/s (M23 max delta-V), peak target <= 1500 g (GSFC GEVS).

We have struggled with visualisation/simulation realism when the payload is
included. With the SUPERball / NASA-TBR architecture (payload sphere suspended
inside the cage by 6 additional TPU tendons), the soft 12 MPa TPU 85A
suspension oscillated wildly at impact and yanked the 0.7 g prism through the
rigid floor in MuJoCo. With the payload distributed across the struts as added
inertia (axial-load model, matching a crutch tip), the renders are stable and
look physical. The bare prism (no payload, just intrinsic strut/tendon mass)
is also stable. A reviewer therefore asked: **for these drop-tests, can we
just leave the payload off in the simulations**, and what does that cost us in
real-world applicability?

Please produce an in-depth, citation-rich brief that answers:

# 1. Physics of payload inclusion in drop simulations

  (a) Which impact-response metrics are dominated by the payload (mass,
      mounting, suspension stiffness) and which are dominated by the
      tensegrity cell itself? Cover at minimum: peak deceleration (g_max),
      pulse FWHM, specific energy absorption (SEA = E_abs / m_protector),
      volumetric efficiency (eta_V), force-time history shape, contact-
      patch evolution, tendon strain energy distribution, and modal
      response (drum-mode of suspended payload vs cell breathing mode).

  (b) For each of these four mounting modes, give the expected physical
      regimes in which the simulation/experiment **with no payload** is
      a faithful surrogate, and the regimes in which it is misleading
      (state explicit thresholds where possible):

      A. Axially-loaded strut tip (crutch use case, payload via tip).
      B. Payload rigidly clamped to one strut (instrumented accelerometer
         mass on a strut, common in tensegrity-robotics drop logs).
      C. Payload suspended inside the cage by additional TPU tendons
         (SUPERball v1/v2 + NASA-TBR planetary lander style).
      D. Bare cell + fictitious added inertia ("topology screen").

  (c) Quantify the regime where a no-payload simulation can be rescaled
      post-hoc to predict the payload-laden response (e.g. via lumped
      Maxwell/Kelvin models, m_eff = m_payload + alpha*m_strut, or
      shock-response-spectrum convolution). Cite analytic and empirical
      precedents.

  (d) For TPU 85A tendons specifically (E ~ 12 MPa, very soft), what
      stiffness/mass ratio thresholds set the boundary between "cell-
      dominated" and "payload-dominated" response? Provide closed-form or
      tabulated guidance keyed to k_cable, m_payload, drop height.

# 2. Real-world applicability and standards mapping

  (a) Which ASTM and equivalent standards explicitly require the payload
      to be in the load path during the drop, and which permit (or
      require) bare-package drops? Cover at minimum: ASTM D5276 (free-fall
      drop of loaded containers, **rigid concrete or steel impact surface**,
      preconditioning, drop orientations), ASTM F1292 (playground impact
      attenuation, instrumented headform), ASTM F2971 (AM test reporting),
      ISTA 1A/1H, MIL-STD-810H Method 516.8 (transit/crash hazard),
      GSFC GEVS-STD-7000B (spacecraft), and any applicable JEDEC (#28
      Lansmont M23 family), ANSI/AAMI, ISO 4180. For each, list:
      load condition, impact surface specification (concrete vs steel vs
      compliant plate), required payload representation (real vs surrogate
      mass vs mass-and-CG), instrumentation, and acceptance criteria.

  (b) What is the convention in published tensegrity drop literature on
      reporting payload-vs-no-payload? Cover Zhang 2018 (icosahedron,
      114.9 g -> 40.9-46.5 g, 1 m), Zhang 2022 (22-inch, 235 g peak, 20 m,
      20-drop life), Agogino 2018 NASA SUPERball, Vespignani 2018 SUPERball
      v2, Anand 2022 (75 m biodegradable), Pajunen 2019 (24-impact reuse),
      Bauer 2021 (octet vs tensegrity localisation), MER airbag papers,
      and BEAR / Snapp 2024 / Gongora 2020-2022. Indicate where the
      drop was with or without a representative payload, and what
      mass-and-CG surrogate (if any) was used.

  (c) For our two regimes specifically: does ASTM D5276 (for crutch /
      packaging) or GEVS (for the NASA-lander regime) require a
      representative payload? On what impact surface (we currently model
      a rigid MuJoCo floor; the standards typically call out a *rigid
      concrete pad >= 150 mm thick on a >= 1 m^3 concrete or steel
      base*)?

  (d) Egg-drop demo path (#46/#47): can the payload-free simulation be
      defended publicly as predictive of the egg-laden drop, or must we
      bring the egg/cradle into both the simulation and the experiment?
      The PR #47 follow-up (`f41b7034`) protocol shared a Ø 200 mm bounding
      sphere, m_sys <= 500 g, m_egg = 55 ± 5 g, rigid concrete floor per
      ASTM D5276; how should that protocol be amended if we want to use
      bare-cell simulations as the screening tier?

# 3. Recommendations and decision rules

  (a) State an explicit rule-of-thumb for when each of the four mounting
      modes (A-D above) is appropriate at simulation-tier C
      (MuJoCo/NTRT rigid screening), tier B (DiffPD/Newton mid-fidelity),
      and tier A (PolyFEM+IPC high-fidelity).

  (b) Give 5-10 concrete simulation/experimental design changes to our
      current setup that would maximise the predictive value of *bare-cell*
      drop simulations while leaving the eventual *payload-laden* drop
      experiment defensible (e.g. always co-report m_eff = m_cell +
      m_payload, always run a 2-point payload-sensitivity sweep, always
      simulate on a rigid concrete-equivalent floor with stated E and rho,
      tie GEVS / D5276 floor surface specs to MuJoCo solref/solimp, etc.).

  (c) For the rigid floor model: what concrete-pad parameters should we
      use in MuJoCo / PolyFEM+IPC to be representative of the ASTM D5276
      and GEVS floor? Give: target Young's modulus, density, restitution,
      friction, surface roughness, contact stiffness in MuJoCo's
      solref/solimp normalisation (current is solref="0.002 1",
      solimp="0.98 0.999 0.0001"), and PolyFEM dhat / IPC barrier
      parameters.

  (d) Provide a one-paragraph defensible answer we can paste into the PR
      saying "yes, leave the payload off for now in the sim because X,
      but plan to bring it in at tier B/A and at the physical drop because
      Y, and here is the floor surface spec we are using to match D5276 /
      GEVS".

Please cite peer-reviewed sources for every numerical claim and explicitly
flag where the answer is engineering judgement vs literature-grounded.
